articles.title: Abu Dhabi prepares for third academy sailing round on 8 November
articles.body: Illustrative photograph of Optimist dinghies on Lake Hossegor, France, in May 2018. More than 40 sailors are expected in Optimist and ILCA racing as part of the academy’s youth training programme. The Abu Dhabi Marine Sports Club Academy will hold the third round of its internal sailing competition on Sunday, 8 November 2026. More than 40 male and female sailors from its Abu Dhabi and Al Mirfa programmes are expected to take part, according to Emirates News Agency (WAM). The round includes Optimist and ILCA racing, giving young sailors an opportunity to test their skills, from boat handling and reading wind direction to adapting to changing sailing conditions. Coaches use these internal rounds to assess participants’ progress and prepare them for domestic and international competition. Academy director Khalifa Al Suwaidi said the races support continuous training and the development of new sailors, alongside discipline and a competitive spirit. He also highlighted the academy’s efforts to attract more young participants and provide an environment in which Emirati talent can develop. The round will conclude with awards for the leading competitors in the different categories. Emirates News Agency (WAM), 6 November 2026 Photo: Tangopaso / Wikimedia Commons, 2018, public domain. articles.title: African Blue Tit
articles.body: African Blue Tit Cyanistes teneriffae Identity and names The African Blue Tit, Cyanistes teneriffae, belongs to Paridae and Passeriformes. French uses Mésange nord-africaine; the mainland form is also called Mésange maghrébine, reflected in the Arabic name “Maghreb tit”. AviList 2026 includes the North African and Canary Island populations within this species, separate from Eurasian Blue Tit Cyanistes caeruleus. Some publications split these populations differently, so names must be read with their scientific context. The species measures about 11–12 cm and weighs roughly 10–13 g; these are approximate dimensions, not measurements unique to each subspecies. Identification North African birds combine a dark blue crown and blue-toned upperparts with a white face, strong dark eye stripe and yellow underparts. The darker crown helps distinguish them from the familiar Eurasian species, but light and age can change appearances. Mainland ultramarinus has a pale wing bar: the absence of a wing bar in some Canary Island forms must not be presented as a universal identification feature. Young birds are duller and have yellower facial areas. Check the face, back and wing together, and retain locality information with any photograph. Habitat, food and behaviour This is a bird of wooded habitats, not an inhabitant of open Sahara simply because it is African. Oak woods, including cork-oak woodland, and other forest types provide feeding surfaces and nesting cavities. Algerian studies have examined populations in oak forests and montane cedar stands. Birds search foliage and twigs for invertebrates and can hang beneath branches; plant foods may supplement the diet. Research in northeastern Algeria found caterpillars important in nestling food. Protecting the insects available on trees is therefore part of protecting the bird, not a separate conservation issue. Range and Arab occurrence AviList places ultramarinus from Morocco through Algeria to Tunisia, and also on Pantelleria, while cyrenaicae occurs in northeastern Libya. The Canary Islands support other named forms and are not Arab breeding localities. Morocco’s checklist identifies a resident breeder; Algerian field studies independently document breeding populations. These mainland birds should not be described as European winter migrants, nor should their distribution be assigned to Eurasian Blue Tit. The Libyan form has a separate, restricted geographic occurrence, not an uninterrupted range across every desert between Tunisia and Cyrenaica. Country and habitat remain essential parts of an accurate record. Breeding and development The nest occupies a cavity, including suitable nest boxes. Reproduction varies with woodland type and elevation: Algerian research found differences in laying dates and clutch sizes even between nearby study populations. Average clutches at some Algerian sites were around 6–7 eggs, with variation between sites and years. After incubation and hatching, chicks remain inside the cavity and depend on food brought by adults. They need a regular food supply at this stage, highlighting the importance of caterpillars collected from tree foliage. The cavity shelters the young until they are able to leave the nest. November and responsible observation In November, interest lies in the daily life of resident woodland birds: where they find food, which trees they use and how they move through the canopy. Their presence is not itself evidence of autumn arrival. Observe from paths, record the locality and habitat, and avoid entering vegetation or repeatedly using recordings to draw birds closer. Viewing the face and wing together, in natural light and from a distance comfortable for the bird, helps reveal its markings. Do not open tree cavities for a better view or pursue a bird returning to cover to feed. Conservation AviList 2026 reports the global IUCN category as Least Concern for the species in its broad taxonomic sense. That assessment does not establish the condition of every isolated population. Conserving mature native woodland, cavity-bearing trees and connected feeding cover is valuable. Research on Algerian birds has investigated nest predation, parasites and pollution, showing why breeding outcomes must be studied locally. Avoid unnecessary insecticide use and disturbance around cavities. A global category also confers no permission to trap birds or remove eggs, and local protection requirements remain applicable. articles.title: Sparrowhawk Hidden in a Backpack: Two Detained in Akkar Raptor-Poaching Operation
articles.body: From the anti-poaching operation in Akkar. Field monitoring by CABS with MECSHAP and Lebanese security forces led to weapon seizures and documentation of gunfire directed at four honey buzzards. In the highlands of Akkar, crossed by migrating birds of prey, one unusual detail stood out during an anti-poaching operation: a sparrowhawk inside the backpack of a man stopped by Lebanese security forces. According to the Committee Against Bird Slaughter (CABS), its team had been monitoring a mountain location in Akkar known for the illegal shooting of raptors, working with the Middle East Center for Sustainable Hunting and Anti-Poaching (MECSHAP) and the police. CABS said officers detained two men at the site. One had the sparrowhawk in his backpack; the other was intercepted while walking towards his vehicle. According to the organisation, the second man had evaded arrest at the same location the previous autumn. The injured sparrowhawk in a backpack in Akkar. Photo: APU The two men were taken to a police station, their weapons were confiscated and criminal proceedings were initiated, the organisation reported. The field operation did not end with those two men. CABS said its observers also documented two other individuals shooting at honey buzzards, two birds each. The team tracked both men to their homes and handed information and evidence to the police for follow-up action. The operation is part of the work of the joint Anti-Poaching Unit (APU, MECSHAP–CABS), in coordination with Lebanon's Internal Security Forces, to protect migrating birds and tackle illegal hunting of protected species. The Akkar case illustrates the value of field monitoring, evidence gathering and cooperation between specialist teams and the security authorities in protecting migratory raptors. Source: CABS

articles.title: Arabian Saluki Championship opens in Al Ain on 7 November with ten rounds
articles.body: An archive image of Saluki racing. The inaugural season brings Al Ain and Al Dhafra together over four distances, from 1,000 to 2,500 metres, ending on 20 March 2027. Al Ain will host the opening round of the inaugural Arabian Saluki Championship on 7 November 2026, followed by Al Dhafra on 14 November. Organised by the Emirates Falconers’ Club and the Arabian Saluki Center in Abu Dhabi, the sporting season runs through March 2027. Qualifying begins over 1,000 metres at Al Rawdah Camel Racing Track in Al Ain. The season comprises ten competitive rounds across four distances: 1,000-metre sprints, 1,500-metre middle-distance races, 2,000-metre endurance races and 2,500-metre stamina races, according to the club’s 5 November release. From November qualifiers to the March finale In the 1,000-metre category, Al Ain hosts the first qualifying round on 7 November and Al Dhafra the second on 14 November. The final takes place at the camel racing track in Al Dhafra on 28 November 2026. December brings the 1,500-metre races: qualifying in Al Ain on 5 December, qualifying in Al Dhafra on 12 December, and the final in Al Dhafra on 26 December 2026. Qualifying over 2,000 metres starts in Al Ain on 9 January 2027, followed by Al Dhafra on 16 January, before the final in Al Ain on 6 February. The season concludes with the 2,500-metre stamina race in Al Dhafra on 20 March 2027. Sprint racing is one of the categories, alongside middle-distance, endurance and stamina races. Keeping sport connected to heritage The championship is held in Al Dhafra under the patronage of Sheikh Hamdan bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the Ruler’s Representative in Al Dhafra Region and Chairman of the Emirates Falconers’ Club, and in Al Ain under the patronage of Sheikh Hazza bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the Ruler’s Representative in Al Ain Region. It aims to support owners and breeders, preserve native Arabian bloodlines and encourage younger generations to participate through an organised racing, registration and classification system. The accompanying programme includes the Arabian Saluki Beauty Contest, known as Al Mazayen, and simulated hunting using a mechanical lure. These activities began during the latest Abu Dhabi International Hunting and Equestrian Exhibition, highlighting both the Saluki’s appearance and its natural abilities. The championship aims to broaden participation among owners, breeders and enthusiasts. A vision for training, research and wider participation Majed Ali Al Mansouri, Secretary-General of the Emirates Falconers’ Club, said the championship’s ambitions extend beyond racing to breeding, training, assessment and research. The vision includes a specialised scientific database studying the Arabian Saluki’s genetic and physical capabilities, alongside programmes to help preserve native bloodlines. Organisers also aim to expand participation among owners, breeders and enthusiasts, and to support activities linked to breeding, training, equipment and heritage tourism. Media professionals, photographers and content creators wishing to cover the championship can access a registration form on its official website. articles.title: As Autumn Migration Begins… Field Action to Protect Bird Flyways over Lebanon
articles.body: Photo: Fouad Itani As Lebanon enters the autumn bird migration season, the Middle East Center for Sustainable Hunting and Anti-Poaching (MECSHAP) is intensifying its field efforts through the Anti-Poaching Unit (APU) and a network of sustainable hunters and collaborators, to monitor violations and help protect migratory birds as they cross Lebanese territory. This action takes on special importance given Lebanon’s location on one of the foremost bird migration flyways between Europe, Asia, and Africa. Autumn migration usually begins in late August and extends to mid-November, with dense movement of birds heading south toward the African continent. Work during the season focuses on following sensitive points along migration lines, monitoring, documenting, and reporting cases of illegal hunting, alongside coordination with the competent security and judicial agencies and cooperation with local and international bodies concerned with bird protection and anti-poaching. This approach stems from a vision that sees the responsible hunter as a partner in protecting nature and the sustainability of hunting, not an adversary to them. That vision has accompanied the center’s path since it grew from within the sustainable hunters’ community, and developed with the launch of the Anti-Poaching Unit in 2018 as a specialized field arm for monitoring, documentation, and intervention, in cooperation with official institutions and specialized partners. The unit has continued its field operations during the current year. In June 2026, members of the Anti-Poaching Unit and CABS carried out a joint patrol in the Baalbek–Hermel area, during which protected wild birds that had been held were received and returned to their natural habitats after their legal status was clarified. (Details of the joint APU and CABS operation in Baalbek–Hermel — linked on the AR page.) Protection efforts give special importance to birds of prey, protected and threatened species, and large birds that cross Lebanon during migration. Documented incidents during last spring’s migration again highlighted the risks these birds face, including the death of a large pelican after it was shot on Amchit beach while passing within a migrating flock. (Incident of the migrating pelican on Amchit beach — linked on the AR page.) The importance of protecting these birds is not limited to Lebanon alone. Birds that cross its skies link, on their journey, multiple continents and countries, making the safety of migration flyways a responsibility beyond local borders, and placing cooperation among sustainable hunters, official bodies, local communities, and specialized organizations at the heart of any effective protection of biodiversity. With the launch of autumn migration 2026, Sayd opens with this follow-up the first files of the new season—to track bird movement over Lebanon, the risks and violations they face, and protection and monitoring efforts—in parallel with following the file of regulating the hunting season and the role of the responsible hunter in protecting the sustainability of their hobby and the nature in which they practice it. Lebanon is a corridor for migratory birds… and protecting that corridor is a shared responsibility.

articles.title: Barbary Partridge
articles.body: Barbary Partridge Alectoris barbara Identity and identification Barbary Partridge Alectoris barbara belongs to Phasianidae and is characteristic of the Maghreb. Its grey neck is bordered by a chestnut collar spotted white; pale and dark bars mark the flanks, with reddish bill and legs. The spotted collar differs from Chukar’s more contrasting black border. It is placed in the order Galliformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour Rocky slopes, scrub and varied farmland provide habitat. It gathers seeds and plant material on the ground and adds insects, particularly for chicks. Groups form outside nesting. Running and concealment usually precede a short, powerful escape flight. Breeding and parental care The nest is a ground hollow screened by vegetation or a shrub. The female incubates while the male helps guard. Downy chicks leave the nest site early and feed while accompanying adults. Walking ability does not mean independence or fully developed flight. Range and Arab occurrence Its native range lies in North Africa, from Morocco through Algeria and Tunisia to Libya. GREPOM documents Moroccan occurrence and geographic variation. It is a resident Maghreb bird, not an equally widespread native partridge of the Levant and Gulf. Seasonality and observation Residents can be observed throughout the year, in family parties or nonbreeding groups. Rainfall and altitude influence breeding timing. In November, quiet rocky slopes and farmland with protective vegetation offer observation without pursuing groups. Ecological role and conservation Scrub loss, excessive hunting and releases of genetically unsuitable stock are pressures. A Moroccan genetic survey examined wild and captive populations, supporting attention to stock origins. Conserving wild populations requires habitat protection and attention to captive-stock origins; indiscriminate releases cannot compensate for degraded environments. articles.title: Barn Swallow in the Arab world: autumn wings between passage and residency
articles.body: Barn Swallow Birds skim a field, turn sharply above a pond and rise towards a wire where others are gathering. In autumn, Barn Swallows seem to draw a line between villages, water and distant skies. Yet the scene does not mean that every swallow in the Arab world is passing through: the species includes local breeders, passage migrants, winter visitors and resident populations. Identification card Arabic names: السنونو الشائع; خطاف الحظائر English name: Barn Swallow French name: Hirondelle rustique Scientific name: Hirundo rustica Family: Hirundinidae Length: approximately 17–19 cm, with variation in the outer tail streamers Habitat: fields, pasture and open country near water and buildings Arab-world occurrence: breeding, passage and winter occurrence vary; Egypt has a resident population Global conservation status: Least Concern (LC) One species, different seasonal lives Across the Maghreb, swallows pass through open landscapes and wetlands, and breed locally in parts of the region. Research on Morocco's Ma'amora bird community documents Barn Swallow as both a breeding summer visitor and passage migrant. An agricultural landscape can be more than a stopover: it may also be where birds begin life before joining a later journey. In the Levant, Lebanon's checklist records breeding, widespread passage and less frequent winter occurrence. The OSME regional list identifies breeding populations of the subspecies transitiva in the Levant and the resident Egyptian savignii. A winter swallow in Egypt should therefore not automatically be described as a European bird that migrated late. In Arabia, seasonal passage is prominent, with documented winter occurrence in Oman and rare breeding recorded at some Arabian sites. Saudi observations identify September–October and March–May as clear passage periods. These situations differ between countries and sites: scarce nesting in one area does not mean that the species breeds nowhere in the Arab world. Autumn has more than one timetable The Eurasian-African Migration Atlas describes Middle Eastern autumn passage from late August to early November, peaking in early October. This summarises studied populations rather than setting a timetable for every village flock. African winter destinations also differ with breeding origin: not all birds follow the same route or finish in the same place. Birds may gather on wires or at roosts before dispersing above fields and water. Recording group size, observation time, direction and feeding behaviour is more useful than assuming that every flock is a new migration wave. European roost studies show that these gatherings also form part of the period when birds build energy reserves before travelling. Reading a bird in flight Long pointed wings, a forked tail, glossy dark-blue upperparts in suitable light, and a rusty forehead and throat are helpful features. The rump stays dark, useful when comparing it with white-rumped martins. But light and distance change the impression: throat and back colours can disappear, leaving an apparently dark bird. Juveniles are less glossy, with paler throats and shorter outer tail feathers. Females tend to have shorter streamers than males, but overlap prevents confident sexing from every photograph. A short tail alone is insufficient for identification or ageing: consider wing shape, face, rump and tail together. Underpart colour also varies geographically, from pale to warm or rusty, with reddish tones prominent in some eastern Mediterranean and Egyptian populations. Belly colour alone should not establish sex, and a photograph from another continent should not be treated as a template for every regional bird. Insects in the air, mud in the nest Barn Swallows catch insects in flight above fields, pasture and water. Their use of insect-rich places makes habitat quality important: a large agricultural area is not necessarily a good feeding area if prey is scarce. The nest is an open mud cup in a sheltered position, often inside or beneath an accessible building. BTO data give a typical clutch of four to five eggs, incubated mainly by the female. Timing depends on population and climate; a European calendar does not establish the nesting season in Egypt or the Levant. Where a nest is occupied, leave entrances and access space undisturbed. Protecting a familiar neighbour Least Concern is a global category, not a statement that all populations are stable. Monitoring programmes document declines in parts of the range, while habitat change, insect availability and nest sites are important conservation issues. A decline measured in Europe or North America cannot be assigned to an Arab country without local data. Watch flocks from a distance and do not approach a roost to force birds into flight for a photograph. Leave occupied nests in peace and avoid blocking entrances while birds are present. Hunting and protection rules should be checked locally with the competent authority. Giving swallows room to feed, continue their journey or return to a nest is a practical way to preserve this shared landscape. articles.title: Black Redstart in the Arab world between local residence and autumn migration
articles.body: Black Redstart A rusty tail quivers above a rock or old wall, followed by a short flight to the ground and a return to the perch. This movement may draw attention to a Black Redstart before its colours become clear. Its Arab-world distribution stretches from Morocco to the Levant and the Arabian Peninsula, but its relationship with these regions varies: some populations breed locally, while others pass through or spend the winter away from their nesting areas. Species profile Arabic names: الحميراء السوداء; also الحميراء الدبساء English name: Black Redstart French name: Rougequeue noir Scientific name: Phoenicurus ochruros Family: Old World flycatchers and chats, Muscicapidae Length: approximately 14–15 cm Range: extensive parts of Europe, Asia and North Africa, with geographically and seasonally varied occurrence in the Arab world Main Arab examples: Morocco, the Levant, Egypt and countries of the Gulf and Arabian Peninsula Residency and migration: resident breeder in some areas; passage migrant or winter visitor in others Global conservation status: Least Concern (LC) Legal status: determined by the country and its applicable rules and decisions; global conservation status does not confer hunting permission From Morocco to the Arabian Peninsula Morocco supports local breeding populations of Black Redstart, with some mountain birds moving to lower elevations in winter. Morocco and Algeria also receive birds from Europe. Local birds may therefore occur alongside migrants in the same season; seeing this species in winter does not mean that every individual has travelled from a distant country. In the eastern Arab region, the picture differs between countries and among populations within a country. Lebanon's bird guide records resident breeders alongside passage migrants and winter visitors. Syria also has resident and passage populations, whereas passage and non-breeding occurrence are prominent in Jordan. Migrants also reach Egypt. On the Arabian Peninsula, passage and winter occurrence are especially clear in examples such as Qatar and the United Arab Emirates. The species has the same recorded status in King Salman bin Abdulaziz Royal Nature Reserve in northern Saudi Arabia, while Oman is included in its passage and non-breeding range. What autumn means for this bird Autumn can bring two overlapping movements: arrivals from breeding areas and the descent of some local mountain birds. European ringing data show movement towards wintering grounds beginning in September, with arrivals continuing through October and November. This describes the studied populations; it is not one arrival calendar for the whole Arab world. A local comparison illustrates the difference. Lebanon's usual autumn passage runs from mid-October to early December. In the UAE, regular occurrence is concentrated between late October and March, with records outside that window. October may therefore be an active passage month at one site and the lead-in to a more conspicuous season at another. An observation becomes more useful when its date, location, elevation and habitat are recorded, rather than simply announcing that a “winter bird” has arrived. Plumage alone does not reveal an individual's country of origin or entire route. A ringing record linked to a documented subsequent encounter can establish some points in an individual’s movement; reconstructing its route requires suitable tracking data. One rusty tail, several appearances The rusty tail is useful but insufficient: Common Redstart, Phoenicurus phoenicurus, shares that feature. Females and young birds may look grey-brown, unlike the dark adult male repeatedly illustrated in guides. Look at the face, breast, underparts and wing as well as the tail. Male Black Redstarts also vary among populations. Western birds may be charcoal-coloured with a pale wing panel, while eastern populations can have more conspicuously rusty underparts. This matters when comparing an Arab-world bird with a single European photograph. A male's lack of a prominent white forehead, together with black extending onto the lower breast in some forms, helps distinguish it from Common Redstart. Females require closer assessment of several features. From rocks to villages and towns Black Redstarts are strongly associated with rocky ground and sparsely vegetated slopes. Walls, ledges and roofs offer some of the same features: an elevated lookout, sheltered spaces for hiding or nesting, and open ground for finding prey. Birds may therefore occur near buildings without depending on food supplied by people. Watch the movement between perch and ground: a short pause, a dash after small prey, then a return to a higher position. This behaviour reveals the importance of a small patch combining food and shelter, whether at a mountain's foot or beside a building. In towns, sealing cavities during renovation can remove nesting places used by the species. Small prey and a sheltered nest Insects and other small invertebrates form the basis of its diet, collected from the ground or during short sallies. It may also eat small fruits. The bird belongs to a food web linking plants, invertebrates and birds. It builds a nest from plant material in a protected place, such as a rock crevice or a gap in a building. A typical clutch contains four to six eggs, incubated by the female. Nesting dates depend on location and population. A bird seen beside a house in autumn is not necessarily preparing to breed there. Conservation and responsible observation Least Concern describes global extinction risk. It does not establish that every local population is doing well, or determine hunting law in any country. Legal status should be checked with the competent national authority, including protected-area rules and seasonal decisions. A game list or legal exception from one Arab country cannot simply be applied in another. Leave enough space for the bird to continue feeding, and avoid following it to a nest or disturbing it for a closer photograph. Record behaviour and habitat, with a clear side-on image if possible. Such details can turn a brief tail movement into a useful observation of birds across the Arab world's different environments. Photo credit: Greg Schechter — Wikimedia Commons — CC BY 2.0.

articles.title: Black-winged Stilt
articles.body: Black-winged Stilt Himantopus himantopus — a long-legged wader, both resident and migrant Name and identity The Black-winged Stilt, known in Arabic as Abu al-Maghazil or al-Karsu, is a wader in the family Recurvirostridae and order Charadriiformes. This account follows modern classifications that separate the Old World species, found in Africa, Europe and Asia, from other stilts. Species limits differ between references and checklists; its information should not be confused with that for American or similar Hawaiian stilts. How to identify it Exceptionally long pink legs, a slender straight black bill, and a white body contrasting with dark wings are its most conspicuous features. In flight, the legs project far beyond the tail, while the black underwings contrast with the white belly. Its straight bill distinguishes it from the avocet, whose bill curves upwards. An adult male has a blacker back, whereas the female’s back tends towards dark brown. However, the amount of black on the head varies and cannot determine sex on its own. Juveniles have brown upperparts with pale feather fringes and duller legs; some of these features can persist through their first winter. Overall shape and plumage should therefore be considered together, rather than head colour alone. Habitat and food It uses shallow fresh, brackish and saline water, including marshes, coastal lagoons, pools and mudflats. It also benefits from some constructed wetlands, including treatment ponds, where suitable margins are available. It feeds mainly on small invertebrates, such as aquatic insects and their larvae, molluscs and crustaceans. It picks prey from the water surface and mud, and may immerse its bill to search for food; its legs allow it to wade without submerging its body. Daily behaviour It is seen alone or in groups, resting on banks or in shallow water. Its sharp repeated calls may draw attention before the bird itself is noticed. During periods of movement, flock sizes vary between sites: a large flock does not imply local breeding, and summer presence alone does not establish nesting. Breeding and life cycle It nests singly or in loose colonies, using a ground scrape or a platform of vegetation close to water, sometimes on a small island. Both parents build the nest, incubate and care for the young. A clutch usually contains four eggs, with incubation lasting approximately 24–26 days. Chicks leave the nest soon after hatching and usually become capable of flight at around one month old. The calendar is not identical everywhere: water availability and local conditions influence breeding timing and success. Where does it occur in Arab countries? It cannot be described simply as a winter visitor throughout the Arab world. Saudi Arabia has resident breeding populations as well as common passage migrants and winter visitors; constructed wetlands have helped its expansion. In Oman, breeding, residency, passage and wintering also overlap. The United Arab Emirates records migrants and breeding residents, including at Al-Zora. In Kuwait, it is a common passage migrant and scarce winter visitor, with local breeding. In Iraq, breeding occurs alongside passage and winter presence. In Lebanon, passage predominates, and the national checklist gives an autumn passage period extending into late October. North Africa has documented breeding sites in Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia, while nesting has also been recorded on Egypt’s Mediterranean coast. Morocco holds wintering birds too. However, a sighting within a country does not establish that all its birds are resident, or that every wetland is a nesting site. Why is it relevant in autumn? Some northern populations migrate south, while others remain resident or move locally. At this time of year, migrants and local birds may occur together, depending on the country and site. Late October is therefore a suitable time to watch for it in Arab wetlands, without treating that month as a uniform regional peak. Useful observations include the date, bird count and water conditions; watch through binoculars from a distance that does not make birds take flight or stop feeding. Conservation and the limits of assessment The 2025 Red List assessment classifies it as Least Concern (LC), under the broad taxonomic definition adopted by that assessment. That category does not remove local risks: changing water levels and disturbance can harm nesting. A study near Essaouira demonstrated the combined influence of rainfall variation and human disturbance. Protecting habitat matters more than relying on the bird’s apparent abundance. References Sources: IUCN Red List, 2025 assessment; Atlas of the coastal and seabirds of Lebanon, 2021; British Trust for Ornithology; Royal Society for the Protection of Birds; Blasco-Zumeta and Heinze identification guide; Hong Kong Bird Watching Society; Naturalis; Mpala Research Centre field guide; The Birds of Saudi Arabia; Official Kuwait Bird List; Birds of Oman database; Ramsar, Al-Zora; OSME and Lebanon checklists; Wetlands International; Wader Study research on Egypt and Morocco. articles.title: How cities reshape bird diversity, and why winter reveals the difference
articles.body: Seagulls in front of Galata Tower and Istanbul’s buildings, 17 March 2015. Illustrative photograph. Photo: MehmetBurakCoban, via Wikimedia Commons. Original image, unchanged. · CC BY-SA 4.0 A Nature Cities study drawing on around 17 million records across 452 North American cities shows how urban bird diversity varies with season and climate. Cities are more than buildings interrupting a natural landscape: they may also reshape the distribution of bird diversity. A study published in Nature Cities on 19 October 2026 analysed around 17 million eBird records, comparing 452 North American cities with their surrounding areas. The team examined species richness rather than simply the number of individual birds, distinguishing native from non-native species and comparing seasons. The north–south difference in native bird diversity was more pronounced in winter, but cities weakened that difference relative to surrounding areas. Great white pelicans above the American University of Beirut campus, 17 September 2018. Illustrative video frame. Footage: Bassem (باسم), via Wikimedia Commons. Still frame extracted at 60 seconds, unretouched. · CC BY-SA 4.0 Season and climate change the picture Another contrast emerged: higher human population density was generally associated with fewer native bird species, but the direction of that relationship reversed under cold conditions. For non-native species, the relationship between diversity and latitude was weak or absent across seasons. The findings highlight the importance of considering season and climate together when studying birds and cities: the distribution of species diversity across cities varies with climatic and seasonal conditions. Sources: Nature Cities study, published 19 October 2026

articles.title: Common Chiffchaff in the Arab World
articles.body: Common Chiffchaff From the Maghreb to Egypt, the Levant and the Arabian Peninsula, the Common Chiffchaff occurs on migration and in winter, with breeding documented in some areas. This small bird reveals how migration calendars differ, and identifying it requires attention to detail rather than a search for striking colours. Identification card Arabic names: الشفشافة الشائعة and النقشارة الشائعة English name: Common Chiffchaff French name: Pouillot véloce Scientific name: Phylloscopus collybita Family: Phylloscopidae, the leaf-warblers Type: a small passerine feeding mainly on invertebrates Arab-world range: examples include Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Egypt, Palestine, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Oman; occurrence varies by country, habitat and season Approximate measurements: length 11 centimetres; wingspan 18 centimetres; weight 8 grams Seasonal status in the region: passage migrant and winter visitor across extensive areas, with summer breeding documented locally, including in Lebanon Global conservation status: Least Concern (LC) Hunting law: check each country’s current laws and decisions; the global conservation category is not a hunting permit In October, a slight movement inside a shrub or among garden branches deserves a second look. The Common Chiffchaff is one of those birds that may pass a watcher without attracting attention through its colours. Its body is small and its plumage echoes the shades of leaves and shadows, but anyone patient enough to follow it can learn to read a bird through its movements, shape and voice together. In the Arab world, an autumn sighting may mark the beginning of a winter stay or a stop along a migration route; the month alone cannot reveal the bird’s destination or origin. How can we identify it? The upperparts are predominantly olive-brown, while the underparts look pale and may show a yellowish wash. A rather subdued pale eyebrow runs above the eye, and the legs are usually dark. Chiffchaffs move actively among branches, with a repeated tail movement that helps draw attention to them. Males and females look alike, so plumage colour alone cannot determine the bird’s sex. The most notable confusion species is the Willow Warbler, Phylloscopus trochilus. The chiffchaff has relatively shorter wings, and the tips of its flight feathers usually project a shorter distance beyond the tertials on the folded wing. Leg colour is a useful clue, but it is not a decisive test on its own. It is better to combine several features and record what was clearly seen rather than fill in details by guessing. If doubt remains, a clear side-on photograph and a note of the voice can help with a later identification review. The chiffchaff is famous for a repeated, rhythmic song echoed by its English name, but an autumn watcher should not rely on hearing that song. The bird may give short calls or remain silent. Distinguishing calls from song, while examining the wing and face, makes an observation more accurate. Distribution across the Arab world The Maghreb forms part of this species’ passage and wintering range. In Morocco, a field study published in 2024 on two High Atlas valleys lists it as a passage migrant and winter visitor. In Algeria, a study of the Algiers Sahel published that same year records it as a wintering bird. In Tunisia, a study of Dyr El Kef published in 2025 likewise lists wintering and passage status. The chiffchaff’s presence extends eastwards to Egypt and the Levant. In Egypt, an environmental study in the Nile Delta region records passage and wintering status. In Palestine, it is known as a common migrant and winter visitor. Lebanon adds a different situation: alongside passage and wintering, its 2026 bird guide confirms summer breeding. A single country may therefore hold breeding birds, passage migrants and winter visitors, with different periods of arrival and residence. On the Arabian Peninsula, Saudi references describe the chiffchaff as a widespread passage migrant and winter visitor, including in the southwestern highlands, and do not record it breeding in the Kingdom. In Oman, too, it is listed as a passage migrant and winter visitor. What does its presence in October mean? Ringing and recovery data brought together by the Eurasian-African Bird Migration Atlas show autumn movements towards North Africa and the Near East, with arrivals appearing in October and more records in November. In the UAE, the February 2026 checklist describes a very common migrant and winter visitor from late October to early April. October should therefore not be treated as a single arrival date across the Arab world. Passage may already be underway at one site while the usual winter season starts later at another. A watcher can be more accurate by linking an observation to its place and date, then comparing it with local records. Habitats and food Chiffchaffs inhabit a variety of wooded and shrubby settings, from forests and their edges to gardens, orchards and vegetation near wetlands. Suitable habitat combines opportunities to find food with branches, leaves and shrubs that provide cover. Small green spaces can therefore be worth watching alongside larger natural habitats. They pick off insects and their larvae, spiders and other small invertebrates, and can catch some prey in flight. This diet places them within the web of relationships linking plants, invertebrates and birds. Watching them search among leaves makes the role of a shrub or green margin clearer: it provides both food and cover. This highlights the importance of maintaining a diversity of native plants and limiting the use of pesticides that reduce the resources available to insect-eating birds. From the nest to autumn migration The species breeds across extensive parts of Europe and Asia, and many populations head south during the cold season. The female builds a domed nest close to the ground or low down in dense vegetation. A clutch usually contains five or six eggs, and incubation lasts around 13–14 days. Autumn offers an opportunity to watch the bird searching for food away from the nest. It is best to stay on paths, allow it to approach as part of its natural movements, and avoid chasing it through shrubs for a photograph. Recording the date, location, habitat and behaviour can make a brief sighting more useful, even if the bird’s identity remains uncertain. Conservation and legal status Globally, the Common Chiffchaff is classified as Least Concern (LC). This assesses the species’ extinction risk worldwide; it does not guarantee the health of every local population. Protecting woodland, shrubs and wetland margins, and reducing pesticide use and disturbance, remain useful ways to safeguard the places where the bird finds food and cover. There is no single hunting rule that can be attributed to the entire Arab world. Determining the legal position requires identifying the country and checking the legislation and decisions in force on the date of the activity, including rules for protected areas, seasons and permitted species. An LC category does not make hunting permissible. Watching this small movement among the leaves and recording it without chasing or disturbing the bird can deepen our understanding of the nature shared by the region’s countries. articles.title: Common Firecrest
articles.body: Common Firecrest Regulus ignicapilla Identity and names The Common Firecrest, Regulus ignicapilla, is a tiny passerine in the kinglet family Regulidae. French calls it Roitelet triple-bandeau; Arabic names include “red-crested kinglet” and, in Moroccan references, “three-striped kinglet”. At about 9 cm long, with a wingspan around 14–15 cm and a mass near 5–6 g, it is much smaller than a sparrow. Its scientific name appears as Regulus ignicapillus in some guides, but current AviList uses ignicapilla. The similar Goldcrest is a separate species. Identification The most useful feature is the face: a strong white eyebrow above a dark eye stripe. This contrasts with the relatively plain-faced Goldcrest. Olive upperparts, pale underparts, two white wing bars and bronze-toned shoulder patches complete the adult pattern. The male’s crown has an orange centre, while the female’s is yellow, both framed by dark feathers. A crown colour glimpsed through foliage is less dependable than a clear facial view, particularly with changing light. Avoid identifying every tiny yellow-crested bird as Firecrest without checking the eyebrow. Habitat, food and behaviour It works through conifers, mixed woods, shrubs and sheltered leafy cover, taking very small invertebrates. Spiders and insect eggs are among its prey. Rather than relying on large seeds, it searches vegetation with a fine bill, moving quickly between twigs. In autumn and winter it may accompany other small woodland birds. This makes a moving feeding flock worth watching patiently from outside the vegetation. Shelter and prey-bearing foliage matter together: an apparently untidy wooded margin can provide useful feeding space that a closely cleared edge lacks. Range and Arab occurrence The species breeds across much of Europe and extends into northwestern Africa. The form balearicus occurs in the Balearic Islands and North Africa from Morocco to northern Tunisia, including Algeria. Morocco’s national checklist identifies both resident breeding and winter visitors, so its November presence there need not signify a recent arrival. Lebanon presents a very different picture: the 2026 national guide classifies it as a vagrant, citing historical records near Bcharre and above Yammouneh. These scarce Lebanese records do not establish a regular winter population, nor should Lebanese rarity be projected onto Maghreb breeding areas. Breeding and development A finely built cup nest is placed among branches or climbing vegetation, using materials such as moss, lichens and feathers. BTO reports a typical clutch of 7–10 eggs, female incubation of 14–16 days and fledging at about 19–20 days after hatching; two broods are typical in its reference account. These are developmental guides, not a fixed timetable for every North African forest. Young birds initially depend on adults for food. Inspecting or separating vegetation to reveal a nest can remove shelter and expose a small brood to disturbance. November and responsible observation November observation is best organized around suitable habitat and the country’s actual status. In Moroccan woodland, quietly following a mixed flock may reveal a resident or wintering Firecrest. In Lebanon, any suspected bird deserves careful documentation because it is exceptional: record the white eyebrow, dark eye stripe, location and date, ideally with photographs that do not require pursuit. A November record from the past is not a promise of annual occurrence. Stay on paths, avoid repeated call playback and never force birds into the open for an identification photograph. Conservation AviList 2026 records the global IUCN category as Least Concern. Local scarcity and habitat quality still matter, and this category is not a hunting authorization. Conserving connected woodland, varied shrubs and insect-rich foliage supports the bird’s feeding requirements. The Lebanese guide mentions illegal hunting and climate change among threats. Avoid unnecessary pesticide use and repeated disturbance, particularly during cold weather. Conservation is served better by a reliably documented sighting and an undisturbed bird than by a closer image obtained at the cost of its feeding time. articles.title: Common Greenshank: a shallow-water visitor to the Arab world
articles.body: Common Greenshank From coasts to inland pools, this migrant combines greenish legs with a bill that turns slightly upwards. Name and classification The Common Greenshank, Tringa nebularia, is a wader in the family Scolopacidae and order Charadriiformes. Its French name is Chevalier aboyeur. It is distinct from the Green Sandpiper, Tringa ochropus: similar common names do not denote the same species. Identification Its long legs are grey-green or olive, and its relatively robust bill turns slightly upwards towards the tip. Winter birds are grey above and white below, with light streaking on the head and neck. Breeding plumage has stronger contrast and darker markings; juveniles show conspicuous pale edges to their back feathers. Leg colour alone is insufficient. Marsh Sandpiper, Tringa stagnatilis, is smaller and more delicately built, with a thinner, straighter bill. Green Sandpiper is shorter and more strongly contrasting, dark above and white below. The sexes look similar, and a general photograph does not reliably establish sex. Habitat, food and behaviour It uses mudflats, estuaries, lakes and shallow pools, including some artificial wetlands. It takes invertebrates from water and mud and may chase small fish through the shallows. It feeds alone or in small gatherings and can be active by day or night. Its ringing call is often delivered as a sequence of notes. Life cycle and breeding It breeds in northern Eurasia where boggy ground and marshes adjoin open woodland or open country. It nests on the ground, usually laying three to four eggs. Chicks can move and seek food early, while still receiving parental protection and care. After breeding, birds move towards passage and wintering areas; some non-breeding individuals remain south of the breeding range in summer. Arab distribution and autumn relevance Autumn is a useful time to look for migrants arriving at Arab wetlands or continuing farther south. Wetland references document passage and winter occurrence in Lebanon, while Libyan winter counts establish its presence at coastal and inland sites. It is a regular passage migrant and winter visitor in Oman. Field studies also document winter occurrence at Moroccan wetlands, while Banc d’Arguin reports record wintering and passage in Mauritania. Egyptian Environmental Affairs Agency reports include it among birds recorded at wetlands. These are local examples, not a map of equal abundance across countries. In the UAE, records are most numerous between August and April along coasts and at wetlands; a few non-breeding birds may remain in summer. Abundance and migration timing differ across the Gulf, the Levant and North Africa. One country’s observation period must not become a timetable for the entire region. Summer presence alone does not prove breeding. Ecology and conservation Migration depends on a connected network of feeding and resting sites; protecting the coast does not replace conserving inland pools and marshes. Globally the species is Least Concern (LC), but the UAE national assessment conducted in 2019 and published in 2021 classified it as Near Threatened (NT): these assessments cover different geographic scales. Coastal land-use change, pollution and disturbance can reduce habitat quality. Watching from a distance, without chasing birds or repeatedly flushing them, allows their behaviour to be observed with less interference. References Sources: IUCN and BirdLife International; UAE National Red List of Birds; British Trust for Ornithology; Palm Islands reserve management plan; Atlas of Wintering Waterbirds of Libya; Oman bird list. articles.title: Common Kestrel — Falco tinnunculus
articles.body: Common kestrelPhoto: Alexis Lours — Wikimedia Commons — CC BY 4.0. Common kestrel — Falco tinnunculus Range: A familiar small falcon over fields and city edges across Eurasia and Africa. Resident or partial migrant according to latitude. In Lebanon and the Levant it appears as a local resident, a passage migrant, and a winter visitor depending on area and elevation. It is recognised by its hovering while searching for prey, relatively long tail, and marked face. Adult males usually show a grey head and tail, with black spots on the back and wing coverts; females and juveniles are more heavily rufous-barred above. The adult male’s spotted back and black claws, when clearly visible, help distinguish it from the lesser kestrel Falco naumanni (Arabic: العُوَيْسِق), whose adult male has an unspotted back and pale claws. Separating females and juveniles of the two species requires careful assessment of several plumage and structural features. Life cycle and habitat: Breeding begins in spring; the pair defends a hunting territory. The female typically lays 4–6 eggs; incubation lasts about a month, mostly by the female while the male supplies prey. Nestlings remain several weeks before first flight. It nests in rock cavities, buildings, and old nests of other birds. It hunts over open ground—fields, pastures, fallow land, road edges, and urban fringes that offer high lookout points. Main prey is small rodents, with large insects, lizards, and nestling birds when rodents are scarce. Lifestyle: Its signature behaviour is windhovering: rapid wingbeats and a fanned tail against the breeze while scanning the ground, then a controlled drop onto prey. Diurnal hunting by sight. Solitary or in pairs when breeding; it adapts well to people wherever nest cavities and open hunting space remain. Dark facial markings and moustaches reduce glare—an adaptive detail shared with other falcons. Common kestrelPhoto: © Giles Laurent, gileslaurent.com — Wikimedia Commons — License CC BY-SA 4.0. Hunting status: Across Arab countries, birds of prey are generally protected and may not be hunted as quarry. In Lebanon, Wild Hunting Law No. 580/2004 limits hunting to quarry species set by the minister; everything else—including all birds of prey—is protected year-round and may not be hunted; the common kestrel is not among the permitted quarry. Despite legal protection, it still faces illegal shooting in some seasons and along some flyways. Conservation status: Globally Least Concern with the International Union for Conservation of Nature, despite local declines in some intensively farmed regions. Locally it may be affected by pesticides and loss of nest sites. Traits: Its hover is a visual scanning technique that gauges distance before the stoop, not a show. A living bridge between field and city, and an indicator of rodent abundance where it is regularly seen.

articles.title: Common Linnet
articles.body: Common Linnet The finch of fields and hedges: resident breeders and winter arrivals from Morocco to the Levant Identity and recognition The Common Linnet Linaria cannabina belongs to Fringillidae; older references often use Carduelis cannabina. Breeding males show a red forehead and breast, grey head and chestnut-brown back. Females are grey-brown and more streaked, and juveniles resemble them. The red becomes less conspicuous outside breeding. A grey bill and white markings in the wings and along the forked tail help identification when colours are subdued or the light is poor. Distinguishing similar birds Females can resemble other brown finches, particularly Twite Linaria flavirostris. Twite has a yellow bill in winter, with a pink rump in males, whereas Linnet identification benefits from the combination of grey bill, chestnut back and white wing markings. Small streaked birds may also be confused with redpolls of the genus Acanthis. Shape, bill, back and tail should therefore be assessed together, with red plumage interpreted according to age and season. Habitat, food and behaviour The species uses open country combining nesting shrubs and seed-bearing vegetation: field edges, hedgerows, pasture, rough grassland and suitable coastal habitats. It feeds chiefly on seeds, often dropping to the ground before returning to an exposed perch. It is sociable, with small groups even during breeding and larger gatherings afterwards. Southern populations are generally more sedentary, while northern birds move southwest. EURING documents European birds reaching northwest Africa, so winter flocks can contain birds with different origins and movement strategies. Breeding and annual cycle Nests are placed in dense shrubs or thorny hedges. These provide cover near feeding areas, making the relationship between nest sites and surrounding seed resources important. Females incubate the usual clutch of four or five eggs. BTO reports typical incubation of 12–14 days and nest departure at 13–14 days. Pairs can produce more than one brood. Breeding dates vary with region and altitude; these numerical ranges describe reference breeding data rather than a single calendar for all Arab populations. Arab-region distribution and seasonality Morocco’s 2017 checklist records resident breeders and winter visitors. Syria’s 2025 review describes uncommon resident breeding in the west and winter occurrence elsewhere. Jordan lists resident birds and less-common winter visitors. Saudi Arabia’s national reference describes scarce winter visits, especially in the north and Tabuk, occasionally also the Eastern Province. In contrast, Kuwait’s September 2026 list treats the species as a vagrant with seven records. Ecology and conservation The global category is Least Concern, but seed resources and nesting cover remain important locally. European farmland research and monitoring link declines to agricultural intensification, reduced food resources and breeding success. Retaining hedges, shrubs and seed-producing field margins helps maintain the complete habitat mosaic. Arab-region monitoring benefits from distinguishing resident breeders from winter arrivals: a seasonal increase in a field does not necessarily represent growth in its local breeding population. articles.title: Common Nightingale
articles.body: Common Nightingale Luscinia megarhynchos Identity and identification Common Nightingale Luscinia megarhynchos belongs to Muscicapidae. Warm brown plumage, a rufous tail and paler underparts lack a mask or orange breast. The sexes look similar; its voice is more conspicuous than its appearance. Separation from Thrush Nightingale combines breast markings, colour and sound. It is placed in the order Passeriformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour Dense scrub, woodland edges and orchards with undergrowth provide cover. It takes insects, larvae and spiders from the ground and leaf litter, adding small fruit seasonally. Males may sing at night, particularly before pairing, but also sing by day. Night singing alone does not identify the species. Breeding and parental care A low nest is concealed in vegetation or near the ground. The female usually lays four or five eggs and incubates for about 13–14 days. Young leave at roughly 11–13 days, before strong flight develops, and parental care continues. Hidden fledglings should be left where found. Range and Arab occurrence It breeds in parts of Europe, western Asia and North Africa, migrating south to sub-Saharan Africa. In Lebanon it is an uncommon migrant breeder and passage migrant. Its prominence in Arabic literature therefore does not imply year-round residence across Arab countries. Seasonality and observation The Lebanese checklist places breeding in April–July, spring passage from March to mid-May and autumn passage in September–October. November follows most usual local passage. An undated song recording without a location cannot establish current local occurrence. Ecological role and conservation Scrub and leaf litter maintain feeding and nesting sites. Hedge cutting, scrub clearance during breeding and pesticides degrade habitat. Listening from paths and avoiding penetration of dense cover protects an unobtrusive bird whose safety depends strongly on concealment. articles.title: Common Reed Bunting
articles.body: Common Reed Bunting Schoeniclus schoeniclus Identity and identification The Common Reed Bunting belongs to Emberizidae. AviList 2026 uses Schoeniclus schoeniclus, while older sources call the same species Emberiza schoeniclus. Breeding males have a black head and throat with a white collar and moustache; females and juveniles have streaked brown heads. Habitat and food It uses reedbeds, grassland and farmland near water, taking seeds and invertebrates. Insects are particularly important for the chicks. Winter head patterns may look different from the familiar spring male. Breeding and development BTO gives a typical clutch of 4–5 eggs, incubated by the female for about 12–13 days. Young develop in the nest and normally fledge after 12–13.5 days. Leaving the nest does not mean immediate feeding independence. Arab occurrence and seasonality The 2026 Lebanon guide describes it as a scarce passage migrant and winter visitor from late October to early April, in wetlands and fields near water. November falls at the start of that period; this does not establish residency or breeding throughout Arab countries. Observation and conservation The species is globally listed as Least Concern (LC) on the IUCN Red List; local habitat protection remains important. The Lebanon guide identifies habitat degradation, agricultural practices and illegal hunting among its main pressures. Quiet observation along reed edges allows feeding birds to be watched without repeatedly flushing them. Retaining field margins and wetland vegetation supports winter food supplies. articles.title: Common Ringed Plover
articles.body: Common Ringed Plover Charadrius hiaticula — A small shorebird feeding through runs and pauses Identity and identification Common Ringed Plover, Charadrius hiaticula, belongs to Charadriidae. AviList 2026 uses this English name; the French name is Grand Gravelot. Arabic sources also use the equivalent of Ringed Plover, while the Qatar bird guide records a specifically local name, rather than an Arabic-wide standard. This compact shorebird combines grey-brown upperparts, white underparts and a conspicuous dark breast band. Age, sex and similar species In breeding plumage the adult has a black face pattern, white forehead, black breast band, orange legs and an orange-based bill with a black tip. Winter markings become less emphatic and the bill may look dark. Juveniles have brown rather than strongly black markings and pale feather edges. Lack of extensive black is therefore not a safe shortcut to sexing. The sexes resemble one another, with females sometimes less sharply marked. Compared with Little Ringed Plover, this species is sturdier, shows a clear white wing bar in flight and lacks the striking yellow eye-ring characteristic of that species. Assess head, bill and wing together rather than relying on leg colour alone. Habitats, food and behaviour It uses sandy and shingle shores, lake margins and tidal flats, and may stop at suitable inland wetlands. A typical feeding sequence is a short run, a pause and a quick pick from the surface. Worms, crustaceans, molluscs and insects are taken according to habitat. Tides repeatedly redistribute feeding and resting areas. Flocks may mix with other waders, but association does not make their identities or habitat requirements interchangeable. Breeding and life cycle The main breeding range lies in northern and Arctic regions and parts of northwestern Europe. A shallow scrape on open ground or among pebbles usually holds four well-camouflaged eggs. Both parents incubate and tend the chicks, which move about and feed themselves soon after hatching. Adults may feign injury to divert danger from a nest; an observer encountering this behaviour should withdraw rather than search for eggs. Migration differs among populations, ranging from long journeys by northern birds to much shorter movements elsewhere. Distribution and seasonality in the Arab world Across the Arab region it is a widespread passage migrant and winter visitor. A November sighting on a beach is not evidence of breeding. Its range includes Mediterranean and North African shores, Egypt and eastern coasts extending to the Gulf, together with suitable inland stopping places. Qatar records common passage and winter occurrence and observations in every month, without those observations alone establishing nesting. In Lebanon, passage is concentrated in spring and late summer–autumn, with relatively few birds remaining in winter. Lebanese winter abundance should therefore not be described as equivalent to that of Gulf sites. November can combine late passage with settled wintering birds, and local counts change with tides and water conditions. Ecological role and conservation The global category is Least Concern, LC; this does not exclude deterioration at a particular site or within a population. By consuming invertebrates, the species participates in wetland food webs. Shoreline modification, wetland loss and disturbance by vehicles, dogs or repeated human approaches can reduce usable habitat. Ground nests are also vulnerable to trampling where breeding occurs. Observing from a sensible distance preserves feeding time and energy. Global status does not establish hunting permission, and European nesting calendars must not be applied indiscriminately to Arab countries. References AviList 2026 — Charadrius hiaticula. articles.title: Common Swift
articles.body: Common Swift Apus apus Identity and identification Common Swift Apus apus belongs to Apodidae. A dark body, long sickle-shaped wings and forked tail accompany a limited pale throat patch. It is not a swallow. Separation from Pallid Swift is difficult in harsh light, which can make dark plumage look pale. It is placed in the order Apodiformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour Most activity occurs in flight, catching insects and windborne spiders. It ranges over towns, farmland and water according to food and weather. Screaming groups around buildings are prominent during breeding. Swifts do not feed on grain and should not receive bread during rescue. Breeding and parental care Nests occupy building or rock cavities. BTO gives a typical two or three eggs, incubated by both parents for about 18–24 days. Young remain around 37–56 days before flight; insect supply and weather influence duration. An occupied cavity must not be sealed during renovation. Range and Arab occurrence It breeds in Europe, North Africa and parts of Asia, migrating to sub-Saharan Africa. Lebanon has abundant migrant breeders and passage birds. Conspicuous summer city flocks do not imply winter residence. Seasonality and observation Lebanese nesting runs from March to July, with passage in February–April and June–November. November numbers differ from summer flocks, and confusion with other swifts is possible. Record head, throat and wing details alongside date. Ecological role and conservation Loss of nesting cavities and declines in aerial insects are pressures. Renovations respecting occupied nests and suitable nesting provision help when food remains available. A grounded swift should never be thrown into the air; injury or weakness requires expert assessment. articles.title: Eurasian Teal: a small duck linking Arab wetlands with northern flyways
articles.body: Eurasian Teal At the edge of shallow water, a teal can look like a small duck among larger flocks. A male’s chestnut head and green face patch reveal a bird connecting northern breeding grounds with Arab winter wetlands. October highlights the value of quiet pools and stopovers, but migration, residence and breeding must remain distinct. Identity and taxonomic scope Arabic name: الحذفة الشتوية, documented in The Birds of Saudi Arabia. The species is Anas crecca, family Anatidae, order Anseriformes. AviList v2026 calls the broader species Green-winged Teal and includes the American carolinensis as a subspecies. This account centres on the Eurasian form Anas crecca crecca, also called Eurasian or Common Teal; its French name is Sarcelle d’hiver. Different English names therefore do not denote two separate species in this treatment. [1] [2] [8] Recognition A brightly plumaged male has a chestnut head with a broad green eye patch, spotted breast, grey flanks and a yellow rear patch bordered by dark markings. Females are mottled brown; both sexes show a green wing speculum. Brown plumage alone cannot identify a female among similar ducks. [6] Age, sex and lookalikes The Eurasian form measures about 34–38 cm. Outside bright plumage, males may resemble females. Accurate ageing uses wing and tail feather details and wear, not body size alone. Small size and the speculum pattern help distinguish females from other brown ducks, but distant photographs or concealed wings may prevent reliable identification. Criteria developed for birds handled during ringing cannot simply be applied to a fleeting photograph. [7] Garganey Spatula querquedula warrants comparison: it is slightly larger, and its brightly plumaged male has a broad white eyebrow rather than the teal’s green face patch. [13] October, migration and Arab distribution Saudi references describe common passage in February–March and September–October, common winter presence in November–February, irregular summer occurrence and no breeding in the book’s account. The UAE’s 2026 checklist lists the Eurasian form as a common to very common migrant and winter visitor. These are national status descriptions, not counts for autumn 2026. [2] [4] Lebanon’s 2020 checklist treats it as a former breeder, with passage in March–early May and mid-August–late November, and winter presence chiefly in Beqaa wetlands during December–March. Pairs seen in May in earlier years were not accepted as evidence of renewed breeding. Tunisian surveys in December 2020–January 2021 documented winter occurrence; the study appeared in 2024 and is not a new count. [3] [5] Farther west, Danish ringing recoveries document birds reaching Morocco in winter. Egypt’s historical Ramsar information sheet for Lake Burullus also records wintering teal. These examples span the Maghreb, Egypt, the Levant and the Gulf; they are neither an exhaustive country list nor grounds for assigning every Arab population to one route. [9] [10] In Egypt, a BirdLife report published in February 2025 identifies Lake Nasser as a teal stopover and wintering site. In Iraq’s Central Marsh, the October 2013–June 2014 survey recorded teal in December–March, not among observed breeders; this is not a current census. [11] [12] Habitat, food and behaviour It uses shallow, vegetation-rich wetlands, including small pools, lakes and saline lagoons. Plant material and invertebrates are taken at the surface or by dipping and upending. The Saudi account describes much feeding at night, with daytime activity too: a resting daytime flock does not mean that a wetland has little feeding value. [2] Life cycle and reproduction BTO gives a typical single brood, 8–11 eggs and female incubation lasting about 21–23 days. Chicks hatch downy and mobile. These are reference biological values, not a uniform Arab nesting calendar. Breeding is followed by movements towards post-breeding and winter sites; ringing shows that some birds stop for weeks while others move on quickly. A duck remaining in summer is not proof of a nest or successful hatching. [8] [9] Ecological importance and conservation The need to feed and rest at several sites makes a connected wetland network more valuable than protection of one pool alone. The Tunisian study describes habitat pressures including pollution, urban expansion and illegal hunting. Such general pressures cannot be converted into a species-specific loss estimate without relevant data. [5] BTO reports Least Concern, LC, for Eurasian Teal; this reference is not a new assessment of the species under its expanded taxonomic scope in AviList 2026. A taxonomic change is not, by itself, evidence of a population increase or decline. [1] [8] Responsible observation Watch from a stationary position at a distance that does not flush the flock, and record date, location and plumage. Reliable identification takes priority over naming every bird: where diagnostic features are hidden, an unresolved small-duck record is preferable to a false species record. This account does not authorise hunting; legal status is separate from abundance and conservation category. articles.title: Dubai Safari Park opens its eighth season with wildlife tours and bird shows
articles.body: Lions in the Explorer Safari area. A first-ever opening week runs until 18 October, with a children’s camp across a park whose six zones are home to more than 3,000 animals. Dubai Safari Park reopened on 12 October 2026, launching its eighth season with a week of family activities alongside safari tours, bird and raptor shows, and experiences introducing visitors to wildlife. The park is holding an opening week for the first time, according to the announcement carried by the Emirates News Agency. Running until 18 October, the programme includes the Little Explorers’ Base Camp, with painting, arts and crafts, animal-model colouring and group games, as well as a stage show performed four times a day and two roaming parades. For bird enthusiasts, the programme includes Birds Kingdom and Birds of Prey presentations, while Echoes of the Wild introduces visitors to animal behaviour and adaptations. These activities combine observation with awareness of the importance of habitats and wildlife conservation. A macaw encounter in the African Village. Safari tours offer views of lions, giraffes, rhinos and other animals in spaces designed to reflect their habitats. Admission includes the Arabian Desert Safari, while the Explorer Safari Tour is available as part of an upgraded package. An Explorer Safari tour passes giraffes. Located in Al Warqa 5 in Dubai, the park covers 119 hectares across six zones and houses more than 3,000 animals from around 300 species, according to its figures. It welcomes visitors daily from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m., with the last admission at 5 p.m. Photos: Dubai Safari Park – archive. Emirates News Agency · Opening-week programme – Dubai Safari Park

articles.title: Eurasian Curlew
articles.body: Eurasian Curlew Numenius arquata — a long-billed visitor to winter shores Name and classification The Eurasian Curlew, Numenius arquata, belongs to Scolopacidae within Charadriiformes. AviList 2026 retains this name and lists its global status as Near Threatened. Arabic sources use “large water curlew” as well as “Eurasian curlew”. The shortened word “curlew” can be ambiguous in local names, making the scientific name valuable when checking photographs and older records. This is a large wading bird, not one of the songbirds that may carry a similar vernacular name. Identification, age and sex Its most conspicuous feature is a long bill curving smoothly downwards, combined with streaked brown plumage, a long neck and long legs. Sexes look similar, but females generally have longer bills; overlap prevents reliable sexing from bill length alone. Young birds can be shorter-billed and should not automatically be reassigned to another species. The Eurasian Whimbrel, Numenius phaeopus, is usually smaller and shorter-billed, with a stronger head pattern and pale central crown stripe. Use the whole structure, head markings and bill together, rather than one distant photograph. Between mudflats and meadows Outside the breeding season it favours tidal flats, estuaries and sheltered coasts, also using nearby fields and meadows. Its bill probes for worms, molluscs and crustaceans, while surface prey is also taken. Feeding opportunities shift with the tide, making safe high-water roosts essential when mudflats disappear underwater. A long coastline is not necessarily suitable habitat: reclamation can remove productive mud, while repeated disturbance can deprive birds of rest even where feeding grounds remain intact. Breeding and life cycle Breeding extends across much of Eurasia in wet meadows, marshy ground and open landscapes. The nest is on the ground and both parents incubate. Chicks leave the nest early and move and feed under parental supervision before they can fly; a chick on the ground is therefore not necessarily abandoned. Drainage and early mowing can reduce breeding success. Many birds move towards warmer coasts afterwards. Non-breeding individuals may remain south of the breeding range in summer, which is not evidence of local nesting. Arab autumn and winter distribution In Kuwait it is a prominent winter visitor and passage migrant, with some summering birds but no implication of breeding. Oman’s database describes abundant passage and winter occurrence. Moroccan surveys document winter use of coastal lagoons and estuaries, including Sidi Moussa–Oualidia; winter records are also documented at Aden in Yemen. Lebanon differs sharply: its 2026 guide treats it as a coastal vagrant. Early November is therefore relevant to suitable Gulf and North African shores, but present-day abundance at any particular site requires a current count, not recycled historical totals. Why protection matters Its Near Threatened status reflects concerns including habitat loss and degradation, killing, disturbance and pressures on breeding grounds. Feeding flats and roosts need protection together. For an observer, repeated retreat or interrupted feeding means more distance is needed. Chasing a flock for a flight photograph is not responsible observation. Winter presence does not imply permission to hunt: applicable law is a separate, country- and date-specific question.
