articles.title: Eurasian Siskin
articles.body: Eurasian Siskin A small seed specialist with autumn passage and variable winter occurrence across the Arab region Identity and recognition The Eurasian Siskin Spinus spinus is a small member of Fringillidae, formerly often placed in Carduelis. Arabic references use «حسون الشوك», while Qatar’s nature guide gives the variant «حسون الشوكة الأوربي». Males are yellow-green with a black cap and chin and dark wings crossed by yellow. Females are greyer and more streaked, without the conspicuous black cap. Juveniles show heavier streaking and less yellow. The short forked tail has yellow sides, and the fine conical bill extracts small seeds. These combined features are more useful than colour alone. Distinguishing similar birds European Greenfinches are bulkier and have much stronger bills. European Serins have shorter, stouter bills, whereas Siskins show prominent yellow tail sides and wing bars. Sex and age influence the visibility of the black head markings: their absence in a female or young bird does not rule out Siskin. Following a bird as it climbs thin branches and hangs below them gives a better view than a fleeting glimpse of yellow among leaves. Habitat, food and behaviour Breeding is associated particularly with coniferous woodland. Outside breeding, alders, birches, suitable gardens and parks provide feeding opportunities. Birds extract seeds from cones and catkins, sometimes hanging upside down, and collect fallen seeds from the ground. Flocks are mobile and vocal, with an undulating flight. Populations range from resident to migratory, with migration generally more pronounced at northern latitudes. EURING documents movements reaching North Africa and the Middle East; routes and annual arrivals vary with population origin and food resources. Breeding and annual cycle The nest is concealed among tree branches, often in a conifer, and uses fine twigs, moss and softer material. A normal clutch contains four or five eggs, incubated by the female. BTO gives typical incubation of 12–13 days and a nestling period of 13–15 days. Care continues after the young leave the nest, and favourable food conditions can allow more than one brood. These describe the known breeding range, whereas Arab-region records mainly concern winter visitors and passage birds. Arab-region distribution and seasonality Lebanon’s 2020 checklist records autumn passage from late October to late November and winter presence from December to mid-February, notably in conifers in Mount Lebanon and the Beqaa. Jordan lists it as a winter visitor, as does Morocco’s 2017 checklist. Occurrence becomes less regular farther east and south: Kuwait’s updated 2026 list calls it a rare winter visitor, while Qatar’s nature guide treats it as a vagrant. Late October is therefore appropriate for watching the start of Lebanese passage, with substantial differences between countries and years. Ecology and conservation Siskins consume seeds within woodland and garden food webs, and their presence reflects tree diversity and seasonal seed production. Their current global category is Least Concern. Winter counts must be interpreted alongside mobility: a flock disappearing from one site may have moved to another food source. Maintaining varied tree stands and cold-season feeding habitats is useful. Records combining species, number, date and habitat reveal more than comparing a single sighting with an entire previous year. articles.title: The European Bee-eater
articles.body: European Bee-eater With its chestnut back, yellow throat and turquoise breast, the European Bee-eater is a striking sight in the skies across much of the Arab world. Its flocks may pass through one country on migration, while other populations remain to breed in another. Seeing the bird, or simply describing it as “migratory”, is therefore not enough to understand the nature of its presence in a particular place. Species profile Arabic name: الوروار الأوروبي English name: European Bee-eater French name: Guêpier d’Europe Scientific name: Merops apiaster Family: bee-eaters, Meropidae Order: Coraciiformes Seasonal status in the Arab world: a passage migrant across wide areas and a summer breeder in parts of North Africa, the Mashriq and the Arabian Peninsula; its status varies locally Global conservation status: Least Concern, LC, according to BirdLife’s 2024 assessment Legal hunting status: determined by each country’s laws and the regulations in force; global conservation status does not establish whether hunting is permitted How to distinguish it from other bee-eaters The adult combines a chestnut head and back with a yellow throat, separated by a black line from the blue-green underparts. Other features include its long, slightly curved bill, the dark stripe through the eye and the two elongated central tail feathers. Juveniles look greener and lack the same tail extensions, so identification should draw on more than one feature. The general name “bee-eater” covers several species in the region. The Blue-cheeked Bee-eater Merops persicus is predominantly green, with a blue tinge on the face. The region also has smaller, mainly green species, including the African Green Bee-eater Merops viridissimus and the Arabian Green Bee-eater Merops cyanophrys. Modern checklists recognise these as separate species following the split of the former Green Bee-eater group. Scientific names remain an important reference when Arabic names differ between guides and countries. Where it occurs in the Arab world In Morocco, the European Bee-eater occurs both on passage and as a seasonal breeder, with occasional winter records noted in the national checklist. A field study published in 2023 documented breeding colonies near Meknes. In Tunisia, too, it is a migratory breeder and passage migrant, although its colonies are not evenly distributed among sites. In Egypt, ringing studies confirm its passage in spring and autumn. In Lebanon, it is a common passage migrant, and there are summer observations, but local breeding remains unconfirmed. The situation differs in Iraq, where it is listed as a summer breeding visitor and passage migrant. Its connection with the Arabian Peninsula extends beyond flying over it: Oman’s official checklist lists it as a summer breeding visitor and passage migrant, describing it as uncommon. Migration and wintering follow different regional calendars This species links breeding areas in North Africa, Europe and Asia with wintering areas in Africa. Tracking and ringing data show that European populations take different routes to western, eastern and southern Africa. Passage dates in one country cannot be applied to all Arab countries. In Lebanon, for example, the scientific checklist places spring passage between early April and early June, and autumn passage between mid-August and early November, with September and October particularly prominent in autumn. The occasional winter records from Morocco do not make the species a regular winter visitor throughout the Arab world. Recording the location, date and behaviour helps distinguish a passing flock from a feeding stopover or a sustained presence that warrants further observation. The diet of an aerial hunter The European Bee-eater catches flying insects, including bees, wasps and other prey. It may return to a perch to handle its prey before swallowing it. Despite its name, its diet is not limited to honey bees, and the proportion of bees in its diet varies between sites and seasons. A field study near apiaries in Murcia, Spain, found that honey bee consumption differed between sites and stages of the breeding season. It is therefore inappropriate to assume that every flock causes the same losses, or that predation on bees automatically strengthens the colony. A more accurate understanding starts with establishing when the birds are present, what food is available and the conditions at the apiary, rather than turning an ecological relationship into a single, fixed judgement. Nesting in the soil The bee-eater excavates a tunnel in suitable soil, often in an earth cliff or bank, ending in a nest chamber. Nests may be close together in a colony. This explains the importance of undisturbed earthen slopes in breeding areas, alongside open habitats rich in insects. Observers do not need to approach the tunnel entrance to confirm the bird’s presence. Watching from a distance allows adults to continue entering and leaving normally, while avoiding disturbance to nests or leaving them exposed. Preserving natural earth cliffs is just as important as protecting the birds themselves. Conservation begins with accurate knowledge The species’ global classification as Least Concern does not necessarily reflect the condition of every local population, nor does it grant permission to hunt it. Hunting and protected-area rules must be checked for the country and date concerned. Understanding the bird in the field begins with identifying the species correctly, understanding why it is present in that season and place, and allowing it to feed and breed without pursuit or disturbance.

articles.title: European Golden Plover
articles.body: European Golden Plover Pluvialis apricaria Identity and identification European Golden Plover, also called Eurasian Golden Plover, is الزقزاق المذهب الأوراسي in Arabic and Pluvier doré in French. Pluvialis apricaria belongs to Charadriidae, order Charadriiformes. About 28 cm long, it has a relatively stocky body, short bill and finely gold-spangled back. “Golden” does not mean uniformly yellow: the appearance of the speckling changes with light, distance and feather condition. Breeding birds have black on the face and underparts, bordered laterally by white; winter underparts are paler. Juveniles resemble winter adults, so absence of black does not determine age. Pacific Golden Plover is an important regional comparison: European Golden Plover is stockier, with shorter bill and legs, and white underwings rather than grey-brown. Grey Plover shows black axillaries. Document these characters when visible naturally, without forcing flight. Habitat, food and behaviour Breeding habitat includes northern open landscapes, tundra and uplands with short vegetation. Outside breeding, it uses grassland, pasture, farmland and steppe, sometimes near coasts. Unlike the stereotypical waterside wader, it may be far from open water: damp ground suitable for feeding can matter more than an obvious shoreline. It takes terrestrial invertebrates, including worms and insects, watching, pausing and moving quickly to pick prey. Large flocks may gather, sometimes alongside lapwings or other field birds according to locality. Frozen ground and soil conditions affect access to food, so its winter distribution is not fixed. Feeding and resting places work together, and a flock can move between them without leaving the wider area. Breeding and development Nests are on the ground and the eggs blend with surrounding vegetation and material. BTO gives a typical clutch of four, incubation of 28–31 days, and flight at about 25–33 days after hatching. Chicks are downy and mobile early, but cannot fly during their first weeks. These intervals describe breeding within the northern range. They do not imply nesting in every winter destination, nor should British egg-laying dates become an assumed Arab breeding calendar. Distinguishing breeding and winter ranges explains why it appears in Arab farmland as northern temperatures fall. Range and Arab occurrence The breeding range extends from parts of northern Europe into northwestern Asia. Winter movements reach western and southern Europe, the Mediterranean and North Africa. The 2026 Lebanon guide lists a scarce passage migrant and common winter visitor in grassland, steppe and coastal habitats. Oman lists a rare passage migrant and winter visitor, making separation from Pacific Golden Plover particularly important. Tracking of birds breeding in Swedish Lapland documented some winter movements to Iberia or Morocco associated with cold spells. This confirms Morocco as a winter movement destination, not as the destination of every population. Kuwait’s rarities committee list instead treats it as a vagrant, rather than a regular winter visitor. What November means November is suitable for searching established winter areas, but the month does not guarantee a bird in every field or country. Record numbers, ground conditions, weather and flock behaviour. An increase after cold weather may reflect arrivals; movement within a plain may simply connect feeding and resting places. Differences between two days do not establish a long-term population trend. Conservation and responsible observation Its global category is Least Concern (LC). Local pressures nevertheless include illegal hunting, habitat degradation and severe weather, as the Lebanon guide notes. Keep far enough away for feeding to continue, and avoid walking directly towards resting flocks. A telescope and existing routes reduce disturbance. Protecting suitable open wet ground and pasture helps winter survival even where a site does not resemble a conventional marsh. articles.title: European Roller
articles.body: European Roller Coracias garrulus Identity and identification European Roller Coracias garrulus belongs to Coraciidae. Adults have a blue head and body, a reddish-brown back and darker blue flight feathers. Juveniles are duller. Its heavier build and stronger bill separate it from bee-eaters, and it lacks their elongated pointed central tail feathers. It is placed in the order Coraciiformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour Open farmland and grassland with scattered trees, wires or branches provide lookout posts. It drops to the ground for large insects and sometimes takes lizards and other small prey. Tumbling courtship displays explain its English name but differ from routine flight between perches. Breeding and parental care It nests in tree cavities or suitable walls and banks, sometimes accepting nest boxes in breeding areas. Both parents contribute to incubation and insect provisioning. Dependence on cavities makes old trees important: available hunting ground alone cannot support a nesting pair. Range and Arab occurrence It breeds across parts of Europe, western Asia and North Africa and winters in sub-Saharan Africa. Lebanon’s 2020 checklist calls it a common passage migrant without confirmed recent breeding. A bird passing in spring does not demonstrate local nesting. Seasonality and observation Lebanese passage usually extends from late March to early June and early August to late October. November follows the usual autumn peak. Dates vary across the Arab region; dated records are more useful than imposing a single regional season. Ecological role and conservation Large-insect predation links it to varied, low-pesticide farmland. Loss of hollow trees, agricultural intensification, pesticides and illegal shooting are pressures. Preserving cavities and insect-rich feeding areas along migration routes supports the species while leaving nests and resting birds undisturbed. articles.title: Garganey
articles.body: Garganey Spatula querquedula Identity and names Garganey, Sarcelle d’été in French, is the small migratory duck Spatula querquedula, in Anatidae and the order Anseriformes. Older references may use Anas querquedula for the same species. It is about 39 cm long. The Arabic name “summer teal” reflects its occurrence on northern breeding grounds; it does not mean that it spends the summer in every Arab country or is absent throughout the region in winter. Identification A breeding male has a conspicuous long white eyebrow above a brown head, a brown breast, grey flanks and contrasting scapular feathers. Females are mottled brown; strong pale and dark facial lines and a relatively longer, heavier bill help separate them from female Eurasian Teal. Absence of the male’s large white eyebrow does not establish sex: males outside breeding plumage and juveniles are less distinctive. An olive-green wing speculum has narrow white borders. Combine head and bill shape, facial pattern and wing markings rather than identifying a bird from a single feature. Habitat, food and behaviour It favours shallow water with vegetated margins: marshes, freshwater lakes, flooded meadows and wet fields. It feeds near the surface by lowering its bill and head, taking insects and aquatic invertebrates, with plant material also included. It does not depend on the deep diving characteristic of diving ducks. Birds may join other ducks at migration stopovers and readily disappear into vegetation. A brief visit with few sightings therefore need not mean a site is unused; equally, a pair in suitable habitat does not by itself establish breeding. Range and Arab occurrence Its breeding range extends across Europe and Asia, with wintering populations in sub-Saharan Africa, the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia. Arab countries show important seasonal differences. The 2026 Lebanon guide describes widespread, common spring passage from early February to April, much scarcer passage from August to early November, and rare summer breeding. Oman’s published official list instead describes an abundant passage migrant and common winter visitor. Lebanon’s seasonal description should not be transferred to southeastern Arabia, and passage should not be equated with established winter residence at every site. In Kuwait, the local reference describes common passage and rare summer occurrence, including birds in mixed duck flocks at freshwater pools around Jahra. Breeding and development The nest is on the ground among grass or low vegetation, sometimes away from the water’s edge. BTO gives a typical clutch of 8–9 eggs and female incubation lasting about 21–23 days. The downy young can move soon after hatching and usually become capable of flight at about 35–40 days. These are approximate developmental intervals, not a fixed calendar shared by every population: weather, water availability and site conditions influence the season. A chick leaving the nest on foot or swimming is not yet necessarily able to fly or independent of its mother. November and responsible observation Interpreting a November sighting requires its country, site and date. An early-November Lebanese record may belong to the end of autumn passage, whereas occurrence in Oman is consistent with the winter season. Watch pool margins from a fixed distance with binoculars, recording numbers, behaviour and visible plumage without flushing the birds. A handsome male’s plumage does not establish local breeding. Neither a photograph nor a better view justifies entering reeds or approaching a concealed female. If birds raise their heads anxiously or stop feeding, retreat and keep their route to cover clear. Conservation Specialist references report the species as globally Least Concern (LC) on the IUCN Red List. This describes global extinction risk, not the safety of every local population. The Lebanon guide identifies excessive hunting, habitat deterioration, disturbance, pollution and poisoning among pressures. Conserving small wetlands, clean water and connected vegetation protects places where migrants rest and feed during long journeys. Compliance with local protection laws remains necessary regardless of the species’ global category. articles.title: Greylag Goose
articles.body: Greylag Goose Anser anser — A large wild goose whose regional abundance varies sharply Identity and identification Greylag Goose, Anser anser, belongs to Anatidae within Anseriformes, with its scientific name retained in AviList 2026. Arabic sources use names corresponding to grey or ashy goose. This is a large, heavy-bodied bird with a strong neck and head, grey-brown plumage edged paler, and pink legs. The substantial bill may be orange or pink according to population, so bill colour alone is not a definitive identification test. Age, sex and similar species Males and females have similar plumage, although males are generally larger; an isolated photograph without comparison seldom establishes sex. Young birds show less developed features in parts of the belly pattern. In flight the pale grey forewing contrasts with darker flight feathers. Adult Greater White-fronted Geese have white at the bill base and strong dark belly barring, but young birds have not developed the complete pattern. Head, bill and wing structure therefore remain important. Domestic, feral and hybrid geese can also resemble wild Greylags; appearance and location alone do not prove natural wild origin. Habitats, food and behaviour The species uses freshwater lakes, marshes and floodplains, together with nearby grassland and fields. Food is predominantly plant material, including grasses, aquatic vegetation, grain and available crops. Flocks may leave water to graze and return to rest or roost. Family groups remain associated and join other birds outside the breeding season, whereas nesting pairs defend their immediate space. A tame goose beside an ornamental pond should not automatically be treated as evidence of wild migration. Breeding and life cycle Breeding occurs across a broad Eurasian range. A ground nest close to water and vegetation usually contains five to seven eggs. The female incubates while the male contributes protection; goslings soon leave the nest to follow their parents and feed. Replacement of the wing feathers produces a flightless period, increasing the importance of secure water. Resident and migratory strategies differ between populations. The existence of resident geese in a European country does not imply that birds arriving in Iraq belong to a resident population. Distribution and seasonality in the Arab world Within the Arab region, Iraq is important in the eastern wintering range, particularly its marshes and other wetlands. Scientific regional reviews also document limited local breeding in southern Iraq, so a single seasonal label cannot describe every bird there. The winter range reaches the northernmost parts of Africa, with strongly variable numbers and regularity. Qatar accounts treat the species as a rare winter visitor, while Lebanon’s 2026 bird guide confirms its vagrant status rather than treating it as a familiar winter goose. November is an appropriate time to watch for arrivals within wintering areas, not a guarantee of occurrence at every Arab lake. Date, locality, behaviour and possible origin should be recorded carefully for observations away from known centres. Ecological role and conservation Its global category is Least Concern, LC, but population circumstances differ. Grazing links terrestrial feeding grounds with wetlands. Use of crops can create agricultural conflicts in some regions, without implying damage at every site. Wetland drainage, pollution, disturbance and uncontrolled hunting require evidence-based local management. Quiet roosts connected to feeding grounds are more useful to the birds than repeated pursuit for photographs. Global conservation status does not determine the legality or season of hunting in any country. References AviList 2026 — Anser anser. BTO — BirdFacts: Greylag Goose. articles.title: Hooded Crow
articles.body: Hooded Crow Corvus cornix — Identification, habitats, breeding and occurrence in the Arab region Identity and identification The Hooded Crow, Corvus cornix, is a member of Corvidae approximately half a metre long. It usually combines a grey body with black head, throat, wings and tail, plus a dark bill and legs. The sexes look alike; size variation rarely allows a single bird to be sexed confidently. Juveniles are less glossy and their grey plumage can look slightly brown. Distribution of colour, bill structure and tail shape are more useful than size alone. Similar birds and taxonomic boundaries House Crow, Corvus splendens, present in some Arab coastal cities, has differently distributed grey and a slimmer build. Larger black ravens lack the same grey mantle. Hooded and Carrion Crows can hybridise where their European ranges meet. Iraq’s capellanus requires particular care: some lists include it within Corvus cornix, whereas OSME treats it separately as a taxon whose independence merits investigation. It has very pale areas and a relatively large bill. Its southern populations are therefore distinguished here from northern grey Hooded Crows rather than presenting the taxonomic disagreement as settled. Habitat, food and behaviour Farmland, pasture, woodland edges, coasts, parks and settlements all provide habitat. This flexible omnivore eats invertebrates, grain, fruit, carrion and discarded food, and may take small vertebrates, eggs or chicks. Dietary proportions vary among places and seasons. Birds walk while searching and inspect resources carefully; some food may be cached. Harsh cawing is characteristic. Pairs defend nesting territories, while groups and communal roosts may form outside breeding. Occurrence at a rubbish dump does not mean that refuse is the entire diet. Breeding and development A large stick nest, lined with softer material, is built in a tree, on a rocky ledge or on a suitable structure. Typical clutches contain 3–6 eggs; the female incubates for approximately 18–19 days. Both parents feed chicks, which leave after about a month and continue begging. One brood is usual, with replacement attempts possible following failure. Timing varies: Lebanon records breeding from late February to late July, while an Ismailia study in Egypt reported an earlier January–April season. Arab occurrence and seasons The species is a common resident breeder in Lebanon and also breeds as a resident in northwestern Jordan. Egypt supports residents in the Nile Valley and Delta, Faiyum and the Suez Canal area: their appearance is not a signal that migration has begun. Northern Iraq has resident populations, while capellanus occupies the plains, date orchards and marshlands of central and southern Iraq. Rare occurrences of that Mesopotamian form in Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates do not establish resident populations. A few Hooded Crow records from northwestern Saudi Arabia contrast sharply with its Egyptian and Lebanese status. Some northern populations move seasonally, but residency characterises many Arab examples. Ecology and conservation Invertebrate and carrion consumption, together with predation on other animals, connect this crow to food webs. Global references describe Least Concern, without settling the status of every population or disputed taxon. Accessible refuse can alter abundance and distribution and increase conflict with people. Waste management, habitat protection and locally evidenced assessment are more useful than universal labels of beneficial or harmful. A single observed nest predation event cannot demonstrate collapse of another bird population. articles.title: Seven Migratory Birds Extinct or Presumed Extinct in 150 Years
articles.body: The last photo of the Slender-billed Curlew taken by Chris Gomersall at Merja Zerga, Morocco on 2 February 1995. An environmental investigation into seven migratory bird species that are extinct or presumed extinct, drawing on BirdLife International data. On 2 February 1995, Chris Gomersall photographed a Slender-billed Curlew (Numenius tenuirostris) at Merja Zerga, Morocco — the last photo of the species. No one knew then that history would record that sighting as the last confirmed appearance on Earth of the bird. Today, with the release of BirdLife’s State of the World’s Birds report, doubt has hardened into a bleak certainty: its extinction has been formally declared, placing it among seven migratory bird species that have become extinct or are presumed extinct over the past 150 years. Not all seven are classified as confirmed extinctions. The report shows that a migration route is not an imaginary line on a map but a “tightly linked chain”: break one link — whether a breeding bog in Siberia or a feeding bay in the Mediterranean — and the whole life cycle of the species collapses. Case files: seven extinct or presumed extinct species A review of the organisation’s historical records shows that six of these birds were lost in the Americas, while the latest and most shocking loss fell on the Eurasian–African mainland: 1. Slender-billed Curlew — the latest casualty Date of fall: Formally declared extinct in the organisation’s latest assessments (after decades of absence since 1995). Extinction scenario: Its extinction is the first of its kind for a bird on the Eurasian–African mainland in modern history. The puzzle of its disappearance exposes weak protection of long-haul flyways; despite exhaustive tracking attempts, its flocks faded as peatlands and wetlands in its likely breeding grounds were drained, tidal flats it used to rest on around the Mediterranean were destroyed, and indiscriminate hunting pressed along its migration line. 2. Passenger Pigeon — from billions to zero Martha, a passenger pigeon — the last of her species — died at the Cincinnati Zoo on 1 September 1914, age 29. Her body was donated to the Smithsonian Institution. Mounted with the notation: “MARTHA, last of her species, died at 1 p.m., 1 September 1914, age 29, in the Cincinnati Zoological Garden. EXTINCT.” Date of fall: September 1914 (with the death of the female “Martha” in her cage at Cincinnati Zoo). Extinction scenario: The twentieth century’s most infamous environmental crime. It once filled North American skies with flocks that blocked the sun and were counted in the billions, then faced industrial commercial hunting to sell as cheap meat, alongside the felling of the deciduous forests whose mast it fed on — breaking its mass-breeding system and wiping it out in a few decades. (Ectopistes migratorius) 3. Eskimo Curlew — sport shooting at stopovers Esquimaux Curlew (Eskimo Curlew), Plate 208 — John James Audubon’s Birds of America. Courtesy of the John James Audubon Center at Mill Grove, Montgomery County Audubon Collection, and Zebra Publishing. Date of fall: Listed as Critically Endangered and Possibly Extinct (last decisive documentation 1963). Extinction scenario: It flew a punishing route from arctic tundra toward South America. The bird was drained during exhausted stopovers on the American Great Plains, where hunters targeted it by the millions for food markets, as prairie steppe was turned into farmland that upended its diet. (Numenius borealis) 4. Labrador Duck — fatal dietary specialisation Pied Duck (Labrador Duck), Plate 332 — John James Audubon’s Birds of America (male adult and female). Courtesy of the John James Audubon Center at Mill Grove, Montgomery County Audubon Collection, and Zebra Publishing. Date of fall: 1878 (the first of the seven to vanish in this era). Extinction scenario: A unique sea duck with a lined bill built for picking small molluscs and crustaceans on North American coasts. The feather and egg trade, pollution of river mouths, and the decline of molluscs under settler activity finished off numbers that were already fragile. (Camptorhynchus labradorius) 5. Bachman’s Warbler — axe victims in winter and summer A male Bachman’s Warbler, in one of the last photographs taken of this species.Photo: Jerry A. Payne, USDA Agricultural Research Service, Bugwood.org (1958). Date of fall: Late 1980s (last documented sighting 1988). Extinction scenario: A small songbird migrating between southern U.S. swamps and Cuban forests. It faced a death sentence from both ends: drainage of swamp forests in its northern home, and conversion of Cuban winter woods into sugarcane estates, leaving it nowhere to shelter on either half of its journey. (Vermivora bachmanii) 6. Jamaican Petrel — traps of invasive animals Jamaican Petrel, adult — illustration by Joseph Smit, 1866 (Proceedings of the Zoological Society of London). Date of fall: 1879 (listed Critically Endangered and strongly Possibly Extinct). Extinction scenario: A seabird that nested in ground burrows in Jamaica’s highlands. The disaster was not at sea but on its return to land: colonists introduced mongoose and rats to control rodents, and they preyed on this bird’s eggs and helpless chicks in their earth nests. (Pterodroma caribbaea) 7. Guadalupe Storm-petrel — islands turned into graves Oceanodroma macrodactyla — male Guadalupe petrel (mount, FMNH 33449, Field Museum of Natural History, Chicago).Photo: James St. John (CC BY 2.0). Date of fall: Around 1912. Extinction scenario: It inhabited Guadalupe Island off Mexico. Goats brought by people destroyed the thin plant cover that sheltered its nesting burrows, while feral cats left on the island finished off adults and chicks until total extinction. (Hydrobates macrodactylus)

articles.title: Hunting Tourism in the Arab Gulf Countries
articles.body: In a three-part investigation, Sayd explores hunting tourism programmes across the Arab world, from traditional hunting trips to accommodation, guiding services and local products. We begin in the Gulf, then move to the Maghreb, and conclude with Egypt, Iraq and Jordan, exploring how these experiences connect with tourism and local development. Source: Abu Dhabi Media Office Camps in northern Saudi Arabia, falcons and Saluki hounds in Al Dhafra, hunting linked to a resort in Al Ain, and game from Qatari farms. Behind these trips are accommodation, guiding, transport and breeding services, while the knowledge and crafts of desert communities become part of a tourism offering with its own visitors and bookings. At Saudi Arabia’s Al Shamal Reserve, a group of hunting enthusiasts can choose a camp for twelve people, with six sleeping tents, a traditional woven tent and a dining tent. Larger groups can book a camp for thirty-one guests, with fifteen sleeping tents, a main suite, a kitchen and outdoor seating areas. A guide specialising in the environment and hunting accompanies the guests. These are the details of a trip built around traditional hunting: where does the visitor stay, who accompanies them, and how do they spend their time in the desert? The Saudi experience, alongside Al Marzoom and Barari in the UAE and Al Jnoub Reserve in Qatar, reveals different sides of a market that combines hunting with hospitality and gives desert heritage a place in tourism programmes. Northern Saudi Arabia: a camp, a guide and products from the local community Established in 2022, Al Shamal Sustainable Hunting Reserve covers around two thousand square kilometres within the Imam Turki bin Abdullah Royal Reserve. Its experiences range from hunting houbara bustards with falcons to hunting gazelles with Saluki hounds or designated firearms, and Arabian oryx with firearms, according to the reserve’s rules and the type of programme. The hunter is a guest… and a customer for the artisan At Saudi Arabia’s Al Shamal Reserve, home-based producers display their crafts and products for hunting visitors. Accommodation ranges from camps to an eco-lodge offering bedrooms, a majlis reception room, a kitchen and outdoor seating areas. This variety makes it possible to arrange a trip for a group of friends or choose a more private stay, while keeping the day’s hunting and hospitality services at the same destination. Source: Al Shamal Sustainable Hunting Reserve Behind the game is a process that begins before the visitor arrives. The authority has explained that the programme relies on breeding game and preparing it to adapt to the natural environment before release, with hunting limited to specified numbers. Through this approach, breeding and field management become part of running the destination, alongside the camps and guest accompaniment. Source: Imam Turki bin Abdullah Royal Reserve Development Authority The local community has a direct place in the experience. The reserve has set aside an area where home-based producers display traditional products and handicrafts. This space connects visitors with local people, allowing them to discover and buy what they make. Across the wider royal reserve, the authority also trains local residents in ecotourism guiding, falcon handling and honey production, and supports artisans and small-business owners. The Darb Zubaydah Winter Festival provides temporary jobs and opportunities for home-based producers to take part. This setting places the hunting trip within a broader tourism activity connecting the desert with heritage and local markets. Source: Saudi Press Agency Source: Saudi Press Agency Al Marzoom: the falcon leads the journey in Al Dhafra In Abu Dhabi’s Al Dhafra region, Al Marzoom Reserve retains the rhythm of traditional hunting. Visitors are divided into groups accompanied by experienced field guides, and hunt with falcons and Saluki hounds, without firearms. The game includes houbara bustards, hares and antelopes, while travel within the reserve and overnight stays in its camps complete the experience. Hunting… without a bullet! At Al Marzoom in Abu Dhabi, hunting is with falcons and Saluki hounds, not guns. Here, the guide is part of the trip’s value: knowing the place, accompanying the group and guiding it through an experience different from a wildlife-watching tour. Overnight options range from the Royal Camp and Elite Camp to the Individuals Camp, while the desert setting allows visitors to discover its plants and wildlife. Since opening in 2015, the reserve has welcomed falconry enthusiasts and tourists from Arab countries and beyond. The details of hospitality add a social dimension to the hunt. Falconers can take their game away or cook it at the campsite, and activities at the destination include camel riding, guided tours and traditional cooking. The experience thus extends beyond the hunting hours to time spent in camp and with companions. Al Marzoom also features in Sayd’s early archives: the magazine covered its opening in November 2015, then documented its reception of falconers from Saudi Arabia and Qatar in February 2017 as part of an experience-exchange programme. This history highlights the destination’s role in bringing hunting enthusiasts from the region’s countries together around a shared experience. Barari in Al Ain: hunting enters the resort world In Remah, Al Ain, Barari Hunting, associated with Telal Resort, offers a model combining hunting experiences with desert accommodation facilities. The operator offers three types of game: Arabian oryx, sand gazelle and the mountain gazelle known as damani. For international bookings and enquiries, it lists agents in Spain and Romania, alongside direct contact with its team in the UAE. Not everyone on the trip is a hunter! At Telal in Al Ain, companions can enjoy horse riding, camel riding and safaris alongside the hunting programme. In an interview with Khaleej Times published in September 2026, Barari’s hunting manager, Saif Al Saleh, explained that the operator provides firearms, vehicles and professional supervision, and that participants do not bring their own weapons. He said the game intended for this experience is captive-bred and hunted under the supervision of the Environment Agency – Abu Dhabi. In this model, equipment and accompaniment are services supplied by the operator itself. Telal Resort, meanwhile, offers accommodation and activities including camel and horse riding and desert safaris. These options give companions a programme of their own, allowing one visit to bring together people who have come to hunt and others who have chosen to stay and explore the desert. Source: Telal Resort Al Ain The link between hunting and hospitality also appears in the project’s investment structure. Alpha Dhabi Group’s 2025 financial statements list Telal Resort among the companies of Mawarid Holding Investment, with its stated activities combining hotel and resort management with the operation of sport-hunting reserves. It is a clear illustration of hunting experiences becoming part of the tourism and accommodation business. Qatar: a journey connecting camp and farm In southern Qatar, Al Jnoub Reserve combines traditional hunting with camping across terrain ranging from sand to rock and vegetation. The model’s distinctive feature begins with the source of its game: it is bred on Qatari farms, numbered and released under the reserve management’s inspection. The Ministry of Environment and Climate Change explains that this approach aims to ease pressure on wild game and allow its numbers to increase. The game’s journey begins on the farm At Qatar’s Al Jnoub Reserve, local farms breed game that is numbered and released under the reserve’s supervision. The reserve offers a large camp with a majlis, four sleeping tents and a kitchen, and a smaller one with a majlis, two sleeping tents and a kitchen. Its services include vehicles equipped for hunting, while the game list includes hares, houbara bustards, stone-curlews and antelopes. Source: Qatar’s Ministry of Environment and Climate Change The programme is booked through the reserve’s app, and hunting methods are limited to falcons and hunting dogs. Operational details include the provision of water, fuel, daily cleaning services and transport of visitors’ belongings to the camps, with shops at the main headquarters. Private cars are not allowed into the reserve, and movement and hunting arrangements are subject to its management’s instructions. Source: Qatar’s Ministry of Environment and Climate Change These details show how work is distributed around a single trip: a farm breeds the game, a team prepares the camp, a service transports belongings, and workers handle cleaning and supplies. In this local network, the pursuit of traditional hunting meets services that visitors need throughout their stay. Where does the value of the trip go? From Al Shamal to Al Dhafra, Al Ain and southern Qatar, some operational elements are similar, while the character of each experience differs. Falcons and hunting dogs are central to Al Marzoom and Al Jnoub; hunting methods are more varied at Al Shamal; and the Barari model adds outfitted hunting services to a resort stay. These differences allow hunters to choose between a heritage-centred trip, a group stay in camp and an experience combining hunting with hotel services. The value of the trip is spread across accommodation, transport, specialist guiding, meals and camp equipment, alongside game breeding and the management of releases. The involvement of home-based producers at Al Shamal adds a channel linking visitor spending with local crafts and products. A destination’s opportunities grow when companions also find things to do. Camel and horse rides, nature exploration and desert stays add other activities to the trip, allowing family members or friends with different interests to take part. This is where organising the whole programme matters: hunting attracts enthusiasts, while hospitality makes the destination suitable for a stay that others can share with them. These Gulf experiences show the practical elements of hunting tourism: an identified location, an operator responsible for services, specified game and hunting methods, and accommodation linked to the programme. At their heart remain people with expertise, from guides and falconers to breeding and hospitality workers and artisans. Through them, the details of the trip become work, and heritage finds a place in the local economy. Sources: Saudi Press Agency, Imam Turki bin Abdullah Royal Reserve Development Authority, Abu Dhabi Media Office, UAE Ministry of Climate Change and Environment, Qatar’s Ministry of Environment and Climate Change, the operators, and Sayd’s archives. In the next two parts Hunting Tourism in the Maghreb Countries Hunting Tourism in Egypt, Iraq and Jordan
articles.excerpt: Sayd investigates hunting tourism in the Arab Gulf: Saudi camps, Al Marzoom and Barari in the UAE, Qatar’s Al Jnoub Reserve, hospitality, guiding and local products.

articles.title: Illegal Hunting Destroys the Hunting Hobby… Beware of Mist Nets, Birdlime, and Night Hunting
articles.body: A bird is freed from a mist net. Illegal methods — nets, birdlime, night shooting — destroy the hobby. Illegal hunting — mist nets, birdlime, electronic callers, and night shooting — is a major threat to migratory and endangered birds in Lebanon, and to the ethical sport of hunting itself. Illegal hunting (“poaching” / al-sayd al-ja’ir) is a major problem in Lebanon. Many migratory and threatened bird species — including raptors, the White Stork, Turtle Dove, and Golden Oriole — are killed during their annual passage through the country. Hunting often uses illegal methods such as mist nets, birdlime, and electronic bird callers, and is frequently carried out outside the hunting season and in spring, the birds’ breeding season. These methods serve both personal take and commercial ends, with small birds sold to restaurants and cage-bird shops. Sadly, over the past twenty years night hunting has appeared as a multi-method practice: besides electronic devices, the indiscriminate shooter lights a tree, paints a tree on a wall and lights it, or uses lasers and spotlights to kill birds at night — especially thrushes (samman) in large numbers — with a clear impact on their populations. Illegal hunting does not only threaten bird numbers; it also undermines the work of conservation advocates, ecologists, and the responsible hunter to protect these species — especially those at risk of extinction. Competent authorities have adopted laws and regulations against illegal hunting, but enforcement is often lax, particularly amid the crises the country faces. Irresponsible hunting also endangers people: hunting accidents and the use of shot are sources of concern. Environmental organisations therefore work to raise awareness and to call for stricter enforcement of land-hunting laws in Lebanon.

articles.title: Among Cedar Peaks and Valley Shadows: Hiking and Camping in Lebanon
articles.body: Camping on a mountain route between Sannine and Aqoura —Source: Wikiloc. In Lebanon, the scenery changes quickly between the coast and the mountains: a village perched above a deep valley gives way to cedar woodland and cool air. Walkers, wildlife watchers and photographers can choose a day on the trail or a night at a suitable campsite. The Lebanon Mountain Trail, one section at a time The Lebanon Mountain Trail runs about 470 kilometres from Andqet in the north to Marjayoun in the south. Its 27 sections cross more than 75 towns and villages. You need not walk it end to end: choose a section that suits your time and fitness, then check an updated map or consult a local guide for the start, return route and water stops. The appeal extends beyond altitude. The trail passes farms, villages and mountain paths, offering encounters with the people and history of the land as well as its peaks. On the Lebanon Mountain Trail —Source: Wikimedia Commons. Qadisha, a valley of landscape and memory In the Qadisha Valley, steep cliffs rise above old monasteries and caves. Walks near Qannoubine and Qozhaya reveal different views with the season and the light. Some descents are demanding, so pick a marked route suited to your group and keep well back from exposed edges. The rocky walls of the Qadisha Valley —Source: Wikimedia Commons. Cedars and waterfalls The cedar landscapes of the Shouf, Tannourine, Ehden and Bentael offer walks, birdwatching and photography. Each protected area has its own trails and rules; ask its managers which routes are open and check conditions before setting out. Near Tannourine, the Baatara Gorge waterfall, also known as Balou Balaa, adds a striking geological sight. Its flow varies with rainfall and season, while wet rock and cliff edges demand care. Balou Balaa near Tannourine; flow changes with the season —Source: Wikimedia Commons. A night under the stars Choose an organised campsite with basic services, or a site where the landowner or responsible authority explicitly allows overnight stays. Wild camping is not a blanket permission. Overnight stays and fires are prohibited in protected places including the Shouf Cedar Nature Reserve under its published rules. Check the site’s conditions and access before travelling, and light a fire only where local rules expressly permit one. Mountain temperatures can fall quickly even in spring, summer or autumn. Carry enough water, warm layers, suitable footwear, a light and a charged phone; tell someone your route and expected return. Pack out every item of litter, stay on paths and respect farmland and wildlife. The best photograph is one you can take without leaving a trace behind. Plan with the Lebanon Mountain Trail Association, UNESCO’s Qadisha Valley listing and the relevant reserve managers.
articles.excerpt: From the Lebanon Mountain Trail to Qadisha, the cedars and Baatara: scenic hikes and practical guidance for responsible camping in Lebanon.

articles.title: Little Egret
articles.body: Little Egret Egretta garzetta — Identification, habitats, breeding and occurrence in the Arab region Identity and identification The Little Egret, Egretta garzetta, belongs to the heron family Ardeidae in the order Pelecaniformes. It is a slender white waterbird, approximately 55–65 cm long, with a fine dark bill, long neck and dark legs. In the regional nominate population, yellow feet usually contrast sharply with the black lower legs. Mud, shade and immersion can conceal this useful feature. Male and female look alike; a solitary bird cannot normally be sexed confidently from plumage. Breeding adults acquire two long, narrow nape plumes and delicate ornamental feathers on the breast and back. Bare facial skin and feet can become more brightly coloured during courtship. Young birds lack the adults’ full ornaments and may have greener legs and duller feet. A white bird without long plumes is therefore not necessarily a juvenile. Great Egret is much larger and longer-necked. Cattle egrets are more compact, with shorter, thicker-looking necks and usually yellow bills outside the youngest stages. On Arabian and Red Sea coasts, white Western Reef Herons require particular care: bill shape, leg proportions and the complete combination of features matter more than white plumage or yellow feet alone. This account treats reef herons separately rather than following older sources that lumped them with Little Egret. Habitat, food and behaviour It favours accessible shallow water: marsh edges, river margins, lagoons, estuaries, mudflats and irrigation channels. Rice fields and fishponds can also provide feeding sites. Suitable roost trees and secure nesting cover may be separate from the feeding area, so conserving one small pool is not always enough. Its hunting is often lively. The bird walks, pauses, runs after prey or stirs the bottom with a foot to flush hidden animals. Small fish, crustaceans, aquatic insects and other small aquatic animals are taken with quick bill strikes. It can feed alone or in loose gatherings while defending a productive patch. At night, birds may gather at shared roosts. In flight the neck folds back and the legs extend behind. Rough calls are most evident when birds are disturbed or interacting. Breeding and life cycle Little Egrets often nest colonially, sometimes with other herons, in trees or shrubs and occasionally other sheltered vegetation. A platform of twigs supports the eggs. Breeding dates depend on local climate and water conditions rather than a single calendar throughout the range. A typical clutch contains 4–5 eggs. Both parents incubate for about 21–22 days and feed the dependent young. First flight is generally around 40–45 days; climbing away from the nest can precede this. These are useful typical figures, not guarantees for every nest. Distribution and regional seasonality The species occurs widely across Africa, Europe and Asia into Australasia. Some populations migrate; others remain resident or disperse after breeding. Arabia receives passage and winter visitors, but local breeding occurs, including a documented Saudi breeding record in 2020. In the Mashriq, Lebanon supports passage and wintering birds and has confirmed local breeding. Egypt combines resident breeders with seasonal movements; Lake Nasser colonies are documented. In the Maghreb, breeding populations and seasonal visitors coexist, including confirmed nesting in Morocco. Presence throughout a year does not by itself prove that the same birds stayed. Ecology and conservation This small predator participates in wetland food webs and responds to the availability of shallow feeding water. Its global status is Least Concern, despite local pressures. Wetland drainage, coastal reclamation, pollution and removal or disturbance of nesting vegetation can reduce suitable habitat. Protecting roosts, colonies and feeding shallows together is more useful than protecting a photograph opportunity. Watch quietly from a distance and avoid flushing birds or approaching nests. articles.title: Northern Bekaa: bird-net removals reach 38,280 m²
articles.body: Loading seized nets during the field operation in northern Bekaa. Field footage of operations to dismantle illegal bird-trapping nets in northern Bekaa. Watch this Short on Sayd’s YouTube channel The Bekaa Investigation Detachment of the Regional Gendarmerie Unit, under the Bekaa Area Command, carried out an exceptional field operation in cooperation on the ground and through information sharing with the joint Lebanese–international operations team of the Anti-Poaching Unit APU (MECSHAP–CABS). The operation resulted in the removal of an additional 17,640 square metres of bird-killing nets used for illegal hunting and the indiscriminate killing of birds, bringing the campaign’s overall total to 38,280 square metres. The missions, conducted over several days, covered Younine, Labweh, Arsal, Ras Baalbek, Mashari‘ al-Qaa, al-Kuwaitiya, Jabouleh, Jadidat al-Fakiha and the highlands of Nahleh. Numerous violation sites were identified and reached, and the seized nets were removed. After each mission, the seized material was handed over to the relevant units in accordance with established procedures. The operation was marked by a high level of professionalism, precise field coordination and rapid detection and intervention. The Bekaa Investigation Detachment also used a drone to survey the areas, spot nets from the air and locate them quickly and clearly, helping teams reach violation sites faster and carry out field interventions more efficiently. The mission was coordinated administratively and in media matters with the Bekaa Area Command, the Public Relations Division and the Gendarmerie Command operations room of the Internal Security Forces. Members of the Ras Baalbek police station also took part on the ground in removing some of the seized nets, as part of cooperation and coordination between the units concerned. A number of sustainable hunters in the Bekaa also contributed the field information needed to identify violation sites and locate the nets. This was not the first such cooperation. A similar operation last year resulted in the removal of approximately 8,000 square metres of nets. It was considered at the time the largest net-removal operation in Lebanon and the largest in the roughly fifty-year history of the international organisation CABS. The current operation, which removed an additional 17,640 square metres of nets over three days and brought the campaign’s overall total to 38,280 square metres, sets an exceptional new field record and underscores the importance of cooperation between security forces, specialist teams and sustainable hunters in confronting illegal hunting and protecting birds and wildlife in Lebanon. The total in the official bulletin In its bulletin of 8 October 2026, the Directorate General of the Internal Security Forces explained that the campaign’s overall total was 38,280 square metres: 20,640 square metres removed in the first phase, followed by an additional 17,640 square metres removed over three days. The bulletin reported the participation of APU (MECSHAP–CABS), the use of a drone and contributions of field information from sustainable hunters. articles.title: Northern Lapwing
articles.body: Northern Lapwings gathered outside the breeding season Vanellus vanellus — Wet fields, autumn passage and winter visitors Identity and recognition Northern Lapwing Vanellus vanellus belongs to the plover family Charadriidae. Arabic names include al-zaqzaq al-shami and al-qatqat al-shamali; the Qatar checklist also records Dahrouj. A narrow crest, dark upperparts with green and purple iridescence, and white underparts contrasting with the dark breast distinguish it. Its wings look broad and rounded in flight. Colour intensity and crest length vary with age and season, so identification uses a combination of features. Habitat and food It uses open fields, short pasture, wetlands and shallow water margins, sometimes gathering in flocks outside the breeding season. It searches the ground for earthworms, insects and their larvae. Short vegetation and moist soil make food accessible, linking its farmland habitat to a mosaic of wet patches and open ground. Breeding and chick development It nests on the ground in open habitats. BTO gives a typical clutch of four eggs and incubation of about 25–34 days, mainly by the female with occasional male participation. Chicks hatch downy and mobile, reaching fledging at about 35–40 days after hatching. Early departure from the nest site differs from acquiring flight. These are general reference durations. Egg-laying dates depend on region and habitat conditions; British breeding dates should not be transferred to Arab countries. Arab occurrence and seasonality In Lebanon, the updated checklist published in Sandgrouse in 2020 describes it as a widespread, abundant passage migrant and a common winter visitor to the Beqaa Valley. Records extend from mid-August to mid-May, especially late October to mid-April. In Qatar, the Qatar Bird Observation Group checklist lists it as a scarce winter visitor. November observation in Lebanon therefore coincides with passage and winter arrivals, while Qatar has a less common winter presence. These descriptions do not establish resident or breeding status in either country. Status varies across Arab countries and should be read from each national checklist. Watching and conservation Drainage and changes in agricultural land management put pressure on its habitats. Wet pasture, open habitat and low disturbance around feeding and resting flocks are valuable. Photographers should keep enough distance for birds to continue their normal behaviour; repeated disturbance flights cost feeding time and energy. The accompanying photograph was taken in Britain. It illustrates the species and does not document occurrence in an Arab country. articles.title: Northern Pintail: the long-necked duck linking Arab autumn to northern breeding grounds
articles.body: Northern Pintail Its name is not the Northern Pintail’s only distinguishing feature: among swimming ducks, a slender body, long neck and pointed tail reveal its shape. The adult male’s central tail feathers become particularly long in bright plumage. The Arabic name refers to a duck in the family Anatidae, not a singing bulbul. Its autumn return to Arab wetlands connects northern breeding grounds with winter waters where food remains available. Identity card Arabic: البلبول الشمالي; also shortened to البلبول English: Northern Pintail French: Canard pilet Scientific name: Anas acuta Order and family: Anseriformes; Anatidae Length: approximately 51–76 cm, depending on sex and tail length; wingspan approximately 86 cm Habitat: shallow fresh and brackish water, marshes and flooded fields Arab-world status: passage migrant and winter visitor, with abundance varying among countries and sites Global conservation category: Least Concern (LC); scientific name and taxonomy follow AviList v2026 [1] Autumn does not have one arrival date Autumn movements begin in northern breeding regions, with different routes linking Eurasia to North Africa, the Middle East and areas farther south. Not every Arab-world flock can be assigned the same origin. In Saudi Arabia, winter occurrence extends from October to March, making late October an appropriate time to search suitable habitat, but not a promise of birds on a particular lake. [6] [7] Where does it occur in the Arab world? In Tunisia, a winter 2020–2021 survey, published in 2024, confirms its presence. In Egypt, BirdLife and its partner Nature Conservation Egypt identify Lake Nasser as a stopover and wintering site. These are examples of documented winter occurrence, not evidence that every waterbody in these countries regularly hosts the species. [10] [11] In Palestine, the Wildlife Society describes it as common in winter and on passage. It is nationally uncommon and non-breeding in Saudi Arabia. Comparing checklists helps avoid applying one country’s status to another; abundance at a site also need not reflect distribution throughout a country. [9] [7] In the UAE: common on passage and in winter, with some summering individuals. This contrast between neighbouring countries illustrates why “Arab-world occurrence” cannot be reduced to one abundance category. A summer sighting alone also does not demonstrate a nest or successful breeding. [8] Males, females and immature birds An adult male in bright plumage has a dark brown head, a white breast with a white stripe extending up the side of the neck, a grey body and long central tail feathers. The slim neck and elongated shape strengthen identification. Tail length varies with sex, age and plumage condition, so a shorter tail should not automatically exclude the species. [2] The female is mottled brown, with a comparatively plain face and a rather dark grey bill. Immatures and males in eclipse plumage resemble her to varying degrees. Against a female Mallard or Wigeon, combine the long neck, slender body, bill and tail rather than relying on shared brown colouring. Precise ageing in autumn remains more demanding than identifying the species. [2] [5] How does it feed? In shallow water, Pintails lower the head and neck or tip up to reach food; on land they pick up grain and seeds. Their diet includes plant material and aquatic invertebrates, with insects particularly important to young birds and during the breeding season. They may feed or rest among other ducks, so a species count must not simply equal the total mixed flock. [5] Life cycle: from ground nest to winter quarters Breeding extends across large parts of Eurasia and North America, often in open landscapes near wetlands. Many pairs form during winter, but a pair together at an Arab wintering site need not nest there. The female makes a ground nest concealed in vegetation, sometimes some distance from water, and undertakes incubation and care of the ducklings. [3] A typical clutch contains 7–9 eggs, incubated for about 22–24 days. Ducklings leave the nest early and feed themselves under the female’s care, becoming able to fly at roughly 40–45 days. After breeding, the birds moult, including replacement of wing feathers and a temporary flightless period; autumn migration and winter settlement follow before the next breeding season. [4] Its value, and what needs protecting The Pintail’s journey connects distant places: safe breeding habitat is insufficient if feeding and resting sites disappear along the route. Recognised pressures include wetland loss, drought and damage to nests in farmland. A numerical trend documented in North America must not be transferred to all Arab populations without local evidence. [3] Global Least Concern status guarantees neither the stability of every population nor permission to hunt. Watch flocks from a distance, avoiding repeated flushing or approaches to a suspected nest. Dated observations and clear photographs can help track arrival times and changing use of sites, provided confirmed field evidence remains distinct from inference. articles.title: Oman's 2003 wildlife law: Protected birds, permits and conservation beyond hunting seasons
articles.body: Royal Decree 6/2003 addresses reserves, protected species, permits, enforcement and confiscation. Nizwa Fort, Oman Oman's legal safeguards for wildlife go beyond opening and closing hunting seasons. The Nature Reserves and Wildlife Conservation Law issued by Royal Decree 6/2003 on 8 January 2003 provides a framework for protected species, nature reserves, permits and enforcement. The law defines hunting broadly to include deliberate capture, immobilisation, killing or attempted capture of wildlife. Under Article 14, a permit is required for hunting, keeping, breeding or transferring protected animals or their offspring inside or outside a nature reserve. Further permission requirements govern collecting specimens and possession of protected wildlife material. The first statutory schedule lists the houbara bustard among specially protected animals and birds. The second includes groups such as falcons, owls, eagles and vultures. Penalty provisions distinguish offences involving the protected schedules and provide for confiscation of wildlife, gear and vehicles used in violations. Article 13 also distinguishes zones within reserves: certain compatible recreational activities may be allowed in designated public areas, while access to stricter protection zones requires permission. The underlying law dates to 2003. This is a 2026 editorial explanation of that instrument, not a claim of new legislation. Readers should consult the responsible authorities for subsequent amendments and current implementing measures. articles.title: Pied Avocet
articles.body: Pied Avocet Recurvirostra avosetta — a wader combining migration with local breeding in Arab wetlands. Identity and classification The Pied Avocet belongs to the family Recurvirostridae and the order Charadriiformes. Its black-and-white plumage and upturned bill make it readily recognisable while revealing a specialised way of feeding. It occurs across Europe, Asia and Africa, but not every population migrates: some are resident or move opportunistically as water becomes available. How to recognise it It measures approximately 42–46 cm in length, with a wingspan of 67–77 cm. Key features are a slender black bill curving upwards, bluish-grey legs, and a black cap with black areas on the wings and back. The sexes look similar; the male tends to have a longer, less sharply curved bill, so colour alone does not establish sex. Juveniles have dull brown rather than clean black markings. The Black-winged Stilt differs in having a straight bill and very long pinkish-red legs. Habitat, food and behaviour It uses shallow water, mudflats, coastal lagoons, saltpans and saline wetlands, as well as some inland wetlands and artificial pools. Sweeping its slightly open bill from side to side through water or soft mud, it takes small invertebrates, including crustaceans, worms and insect larvae. It may also pick prey directly. Feeding takes place by day and sometimes at night. Outside the breeding season, birds gather in flocks to feed and rest; a flock’s presence does not establish year-round residence. Occurrence in Arab countries In Morocco it is a common passage migrant and winter visitor, with local breeding. Northeastern Algeria supports resident breeding populations, while Tunisia has documented breeding and wintering in its wetlands. Egypt receives passage migrants and winter visitors, including in northern Sinai and the Nile Delta. Iraq supports residents and winter visitors, with breeding documented in the southern marshes. In Saudi Arabia it is an uncommon passage migrant and winter visitor, breeding in small numbers in the Eastern Province. In Kuwait passage is uncommon but winter occurrence is common; in Oman it is a fairly common passage migrant and winter visitor. In the United Arab Emirates it occurs mainly from September to March, with highly localised, variable winter numbers and documented small-scale breeding. In Lebanon it is a scarce passage migrant and a rare winter visitor, not a widespread resident. What does late October mean? This period coincides with the end of the documented autumn passage window in Saudi Arabia and Lebanon, and falls within the usual season of occurrence in the UAE. The Saudi reference defines winter as November–February. The species therefore suits an autumn feature, but one arrival date cannot be applied across the Arab world, nor does every sighting demonstrate wintering or breeding. Actual occurrence remains dependent on the site, water and food. Breeding and life cycle The pair makes a shallow scrape on open ground near water or on a low island, sometimes nesting in a colony. A typical clutch contains 3–4 eggs; both parents incubate and care for the young. BTO gives typical incubation of 23–25 days and fledging at 35–42 days after hatching: reference values, not a fixed timetable for every population. Downy chicks leave the nest early and feed themselves under parental protection. Birds typically begin breeding at two years old. Conservation and responsible observation The global Red List assessment places the species in Least Concern (LC), with its worldwide population trend unknown; this does not mean local threats are absent. Wetland loss, pollution and disturbance affect it, while ground nests face flooding and predation. Observe from a suitable distance without entering flocks or approaching nests and chicks. Protecting feeding and resting habitat matters as much as protecting breeding sites. articles.title: Red-crested Pochard
articles.body: Red-crested Pochard Netta rufina Identification and plumages The Red-crested Pochard, Netta rufina, is a substantial diving duck whose breeding male has an unusually rounded orange-rust head and a vivid red bill. The black breast and pale flanks strengthen the contrast. The female is much quieter in colour: brown above, with pale cheeks beneath a darker cap. The rounded head is as useful as the colour when birds are seen among other ducks. The species belongs to the Anatidae, but its feeding repertoire is broader than the word “diving” might suggest. Body length is about 53–57 cm. Common Pochard males also have reddish heads, but their grey body and dark bill produce a different overall pattern. Female Red-crested Pochards have a dark bill with pink near its tip; juveniles have an entirely dark bill. Males in eclipse become female-like but retain the red bill and eye. These features are more reliable than judging sex from subdued plumage alone. In flight, a broad white wing stripe and pale underwings are conspicuous. Wetlands and feeding Lakes and lagoons with abundant aquatic plants and sheltered, vegetated margins are characteristic habitats. The species uses fresh as well as brackish water and may visit deltas and estuaries, particularly outside the nesting season. A reed-fringed lake offers different resources at once: open water for resting, submerged plants for feeding, and concealed margins for nesting and broods. The mere presence of water is therefore a poor substitute for the structural variety of a functioning wetland. Roots, seeds and other parts of aquatic plants dominate the diet. The birds can dive, reach down from the surface or tip forward with the hindquarters raised. Aquatic invertebrates and occasional small vertebrates supplement the plant food. These different techniques let the duck exploit food at several depths. Water management that removes submerged vegetation or repeatedly exposes feeding areas can alter the usefulness of a site even when a sizeable pool remains. Breeding and the annual cycle The female builds a nest of vegetation and down within protective cover near water. In Spain, SEO/BirdLife places the breeding season broadly between April and August, especially the central months; this calendar should not be transferred unchanged across the range. Its account gives a typical clutch of 8–10 eggs and incubation by the female lasting 26–28 days. Females sometimes lay in other ducks' nests, so the eggs found together need not all come from one mother. Ducklings leave the nest soon after hatching and feed themselves under the female's care. SEO/BirdLife describes a chick-development period of 45–50 days, without explicitly identifying this as the age of first flight. Adults also undergo a wing moult that temporarily prevents flight. Some move to separate moulting waters, where undisturbed open water and cover are especially valuable. Thus breeding, brood-rearing and moulting can use different parts of the wetland network. Global range and movements The natural range extends through parts of Europe and western and central Asia. The EURING/CMS migration atlas describes a mixture of resident populations, short-distance movements and longer seasonal migrations. European birds may winter around the Mediterranean, Black Sea and Caspian Sea; the wider winter range reaches the Indian subcontinent. Individuals do not all follow one route or share a single departure calendar. The species is widely kept in waterfowl collections, and some European populations, notably in Britain, have an introduced origin. Assessing an exceptional sighting therefore includes checking rings, behaviour and the circumstances of arrival, as identification alone cannot establish wild origin. Arab countries: breeding, wintering and dated records Morocco holds documented breeding sites as well as wintering birds. The North African literature identifies Sidi Boughaba, the lower Loukkos wetlands and other localities among its breeding areas. Algeria has both historical nesting evidence and rare winter occurrence. Boutabia and colleagues documented a female with ducklings at Mekhada marsh in June 2025, establishing breeding in the El Kala wetland complex; this was a regional confirmation, not the first breeding record for all Algeria. Tunisia can no longer be described solely through older accounts of rare winter visits. Hamza, Dlensi and Chokri reported two breeding pairs at Khniss during 2025 in Go-South Bulletin in 2026, presenting this as the country's first confirmed nesting. That finding demonstrates local breeding, not a large established national population. Iraq's checklist by Salim and colleagues describes a very local breeding resident in the southern marshes, alongside more widespread but generally uncommon winter and passage occurrence. Syria's 2008 checklist documents nesting at Sabkhat al-Jabbul in 2005 and winter presence in suitable waters. These dated sources establish different national patterns; they should not be read as a current census of either country's breeding population. Egypt's EORC checklist of 2019 includes the species in category A, establishing accepted wild occurrence after 1950 without assigning a season. The CMS account also lists records from Lebanon, Libya, Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates; no seasonal pattern is inferred here from that inclusion. Qatar is classified as a vagrant destination. The Birds of Saudi Arabia describes a rare winter visitor and a rare, erratic summer visitor in Saudi Arabia; summer occurrence does not itself establish breeding. Oman's national list, compiled by the Oman Bird Records Committee, gives a different and more specific status: a rare to uncommon passage migrant and winter visitor. This national assessment is preferable to the broader CMS vagrant label for Oman. Conservation and responsible observation The global category reported by BTO is Least Concern. Local breeding concentrations can nevertheless be vulnerable to drainage, deteriorating water quality, hunting and disruptive changes in water level. Global status and the condition of an individual marsh answer different questions. The recent North African studies emphasise habitat protection and sound water management rather than treating a new nest record as proof that the species is secure. Observe from existing paths or hides and keep clear of broods and concealed shoreline nests. Record a count, date, precise locality and observed behaviour; distinguish a pair, a downy brood and a fully grown juvenile. Repeated observations from a distance are more informative than repeated approaches. Maintaining vegetation and undisturbed water serves this duck throughout its life cycle, not only when the colourful male is most conspicuous. articles.title: The Red-footed Falcon… Killed by the Ignorance of Indiscriminate Shooters
articles.body: Red-footed Falcon (Falco vespertinus) — not the Common Kestrel. While conservation science invests heavily in bird protection elsewhere, ignorance at home still kills protected raptors that are neither game nor food. This bird is the Red-footed Falcon (Falco vespertinus) — not the Common Kestrel. While the West undertakes painstaking studies, intensive workshops, long hours of monitoring, and heavy spending to preserve natural balance through bird conservation and sustainable living, the ignorant among us — whose minds have never been touched by the light of knowledge — kill any bird without knowing its role or ecological importance. They disregard every law, faith, and ethic, expressing sick psychologies that have not risen to the level of humanity but sink to brutal assault on God’s creatures… These killed birds are not hunting quarry and are not eaten. This is a falcon known locally as lazeeq or red uwaisaq; its scientific name is Falco vespertinus, in English the Red-footed Falcon. It is a falcon belonging to the falcon family Falconidae.
