articles.title: Red Knot
articles.body: Red Knot Calidris canutus Identity and names Red Knot, Bécasseau maubèche in French, is Calidris canutus, a wader in Scolopacidae and the order Charadriiformes. About 24 cm long, it breeds in the High Arctic and migrates between tundra and distant coasts. Its name can mislead observers searching in winter: the brick-red colouring is a feature of breeding plumage, whereas most winter birds are grey above with pale underparts. Identification It is stocky, with relatively short dark legs and a straight, medium-length black bill rather than the long curved bill of some other sandpipers. Breeding birds develop red faces, breasts and underparts and more patterned upperparts. In winter the upperparts are pale grey and the underside white; juveniles have outlined, scalloped-looking feather edges. Males and females look similar during ordinary field observation, so colour alone should not be used to assign sex. Identification against other sandpipers requires size, structure and bill shape together, allowing for age, plumage and viewing distance. Habitat, food and behaviour Outside breeding, it uses sandy shores, tidal mudflats, estuaries and bays exposed at low tide. It picks or probes for small molluscs, crustaceans, marine worms and other invertebrates. Food changes on the tundra, where birds exploit insects during the short season. Flocks move between feeding flats and roosts as the water rises. Their habitat requirements therefore include two complementary elements: productive feeding surfaces and quiet places where they can wait through high tide without repeated displacement. Range and Arab occurrence Different populations follow several flyways and use coasts worldwide; they are not a single uniform winter population. In the Arab region, Banc d’Arguin in Mauritania is a particularly important wintering site. Tracking research there has documented birds returning to the same roosts and using relatively local feeding areas. This contrasts with extreme rarity farther east: the 2026 Lebanon guide treats it as a vagrant, citing a bird at Khaldeh pool on 2 April 1955, and Oman’s published list also calls it a vagrant. Eastern rarity should not be projected onto the Arab Atlantic coast, nor Mauritania’s importance onto every Arab beach. Breeding and development The female lays in a shallow ground nest on the tundra. BTO gives a typical clutch of four eggs, incubation by both parents for about 21–22 days and flight capability at approximately 18–20 days after hatching. The downy chicks can move early, but development still depends on food and protection. These are reference intervals, with estimates varying between studies and populations. They do not imply that the species nests on Arab wintering shores: its presence there belongs to a different part of its annual cycle. November and responsible observation November at Banc d’Arguin falls within use of non-breeding habitat, not evidence of local nesting. A bird in an area where it is rare deserves careful notes, clear photographs and specialist review, without pursuing the flock. Record the tidal stage, numbers, bill shape and plumage while maintaining a distance that avoids repeated flushing. Do not walk directly towards roosting groups or position vehicles between birds and water. Good observation leaves birds feeding and resting normally; it is not measured by the closeness of a photograph or the spectacle of a flock taking flight. Conservation The global category is Near Threatened (NT), not Least Concern. Conservation depends on the continued availability of linked migration, feeding and resting sites. Pressures include loss and deterioration of coastal habitats, climate change, pollution, disturbance and depletion of shellfish resources in some regions. A study of Banc d’Arguin’s waterbird community between 1980 and 2017 found a significant decline in Red Knot numbers; that is a finding for the study period, not a new 2026 census. Protecting one important stopover cannot compensate fully for losing another on the same migration route. articles.title: Regulating Hunting Protects Wildlife… Banning It Worsens the Crisis
articles.body: Science-based regulation, with sustainable hunters as partners. Lebanon’s experience of blanket hunting bans showed they do not stop violations — they push them into more dangerous forms. Science-based regulation, with sustainable hunters as partners, is the balanced path. Lebanon’s experience of banning hunting in recent years has proven ineffective. It did not stop violations; it transformed them into more dangerous patterns. A wide segment of indiscriminate shooters (qawwasin) emerged who use cheap guns that are easy to replace when confiscated, while mist-netting and liming rose by more than 70% — methods far more lethal to birds and harder to detect than shotgun hunting. This reality weakened deterrence, opened the door to illegal hunting, and burned bridges with sustainable hunters who could have been partners in protection. A total ban also ignored the social and economic dimension of rural communities, increasing resistance to the law and deepening secret practices. Scientific regulation of hunting is the balanced solution: setting seasons that do not conflict with bird breeding; listing prohibited species on the basis of Red Lists and international agreements; banning abusive methods such as mist nets, birdlime, and electronic callers; and limiting take to traditional individual means. Cooperation with sustainable hunters has proven effective: most violations were detected thanks to their work with the Anti-Poaching Unit, composed of hunters who operate alongside the army and security forces in monitoring, documentation, and filing cases before the environmental public prosecutor. Field work has also documented wildlife and enriched scientific knowledge of bird status. The fundamental solution lies in establishing responsible hunting areas managed under the oversight of the relevant ministries, municipalities, and sustainable hunters — so that hunting shifts from a drain on nature to a genuine means of protecting it.

articles.title: Sanderling
articles.body: Sanderling Calidris alba Name and identity Sanderling, Calidris alba, belongs to Scolopacidae within Charadriiformes. Lebanon’s 2026 guide uses al-durayja al-bayda; Kuwait’s reference gives al-madruwan. The local Kuwaiti name Irhaiz applies to several waders and cannot document the species on its own. AviList 2026 retains the scientific name. A winter bird resembles a pale ball running over wet sand, following the retreating water before withdrawing from the next wave. The scene connects a warm Arab beach with a very different landscape: Arctic plains where it spends its short breeding season. Plumage, age and identification It is plump, with a relatively short straight black bill and black legs. Winter adults are pale grey above and white below with a darker shoulder area. Breeding plumage brings rusty tones and dark mottling to head, breast and back, while the belly remains white. Juveniles have more strongly black-and-white patterned upperparts than winter adults. The sexes look similar, so plumage state and possible age are more useful than an unsupported sex assignment. The foot lacks the hind toe found in most sandpipers, but examining it never justifies disturbance. A broad white wing bar appears in flight. Compared with Dunlin, its bill is shorter and less curved and its winter appearance whiter; shape and behaviour complete the identification. Habitat and food Outside breeding it particularly uses sandy beaches, also visiting mudflats, saltpans and some inland water margins on passage. It takes worms, crustaceans, molluscs and other small prey at or below the sand surface; diet changes with habitat, and insects become important on northern breeding grounds. Running beside the surf provides access to ground briefly exposed by retreating water. Birds may gather to rest when feeding space shrinks. Suitable coastline combines food with a quiet resting place; repeated chasing reduces the time available for foraging. Breeding and life cycle It nests in Arctic tundra in a simple ground scrape lined with plant material, usually laying three or four eggs. BTO gives typical incubation of 24–27 days and about 16–18 days to flight. Mating and parental arrangements vary: both parents may participate or one may care for the brood. Downy chicks can move and pick up food, while still needing protection and warmth from the attending parent. Leaving the scrape precedes flight and does not mean independence. After breeding, birds move to temperate and tropical coasts; some non-breeders remain away from the tundra in summer. Such presence does not prove nesting where they are seen. Arab occurrence and season Its Arab occurrence includes North African countries, Egypt, Sudan, the Levant and Gulf states, extending to Djibouti, Somalia and Comoros. This breadth highlights the value of Arab coasts, but a country occurrence record alone establishes neither season nor abundance on every beach. Lebanon’s 2026 guide describes scarce passage on sandy shores, mudflats, saltpans and wetland margins. Kuwait records common passage and winter visitation, with scarce summer occurrence; Oman’s database describes abundant passage and wintering. November observation is therefore especially appropriate along Gulf and Omani shores; common winter status there should not automatically be applied to Lebanon. Conservation and watching Its global status is Least Concern, LC, in the 2024 Red List assessment and AviList 2026. Habitat loss, oil pollution and disturbance remain important at individual sites. Protecting the wet feeding strip and connected resting places lets birds meet their needs without repeated forced flights. Wait at a suitable distance rather than walking towards the flock, and do not stand between it and feeding ground. Record numbers, time and tide: changing water levels may explain movement between locations. Natural behaviour is more informative than a photograph obtained by forcing birds to flee. articles.title: International Saudi Falcons and Hunting Exhibition Opens Its Doors Until 10 October
articles.body: A falcon on a falconer’s hand during the opening night of the auction held at the exhibition. Ten days bring together falconry, hunting, travel and adventure, allowing visitors to discover a living heritage passed down through generations. The International Saudi Falcons and Hunting Exhibition 2026 opened on 1 October. Organized by the National Center for Falcons in Malham, north of Riyadh, it continues until the tenth of the month. The falcon remains at the heart of the event, with a programme featuring falcon auctions, the ‘Future Falconer’ experience and the ‘Shalayel’ museum, alongside shooting, sea fishing, safaris and outdoor travel equipment. Visitors can meet falconers and specialists and learn about their skills and the equipment used in their pursuit. Among the anticipated competitions is the Al-Melwah race, scheduled for 4–9 October, where spectators can watch the falcons’ speed and the skills involved in training them. Al-Hamad Falcon Draws Attention on the Auction’s Opening Night A falconer holds a falcon before the auction audience inside the exhibition. The auction held inside the exhibition saw the sale of a young peregrine falcon captured in Al-Hamad in the Northern Borders region by Abdullah Radi Al-Anazi and Mashhour Ayed Al-Anazi. Bidding began at SAR 30,000 and ended with the falcon selling for SAR 101,000. The auction is restricted to young migratory peregrine falcons captured within the Kingdom. Adult peregrines and saker falcons are excluded to support the sustainability of their populations. The exhibition welcomes visitors daily from 2 p.m. to 11 p.m. at the Riyadh Exhibition and Convention Center in Malham, north of Riyadh.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia Launches the Sixth Hunting Season and Tightens the Rules: 5,000 Riyals Fine for Prohibited Places
articles.body: The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia launched the wild hunting season for 2026–2027, in an experience entering its sixth year and continuing to develop a model that organizes hunting practice and links it to wildlife protection and the sustainability of its resources. The National Center for Wildlife (NCW) announced that the season, which began on 1 September, runs until 31 January 2027 and is limited to the species, locations, and means allowed under approved regulations and controls. The current season sees a measured expansion compared with previous seasons: the number of species allowed for hunting rose to 30; the national hunting quota increased by 11%; and the number of licenses rose by 34%—adjustments the center says are based on monitoring results, studies, and evaluation of the previous five seasons. Holders of licensed hunting guns of the allowed types—air and gas guns that operate without gunpowder—as well as falconers registered with the Saudi Falcons Club, must obtain hunting permits electronically via the “Fitri” platform. Issuing licenses to hunt allowed species with falcons has also become linked to the existence of a falcon ownership certificate or passport. In parallel, the permanent ban on hunting endangered wildlife species continues, and hunting is prohibited inside cities, villages, farms, rest houses, and population gatherings, and inside protected areas and major projects—including NEOM, Qiddiya, and the Red Sea Project—in addition to a belt extending 20 kilometers inland from the Kingdom’s coasts. The regulations also ban hunting means that allow catching more than one animal at the same time, including shotguns and nets, as well as unauthorized attraction and calling methods. The National Center for Wildlife (NCW) considers that the previous five seasons made it possible to build a base of data and experience that helps set species, quotas, and licenses according to species’ status and capacity to renew. The center’s CEO, Dr. Mohammed Ali Qurban, affirmed that the lawful hunter is a partner in wildlife sustainability, stressing that regulating hunting allows the practice to continue, while random and excessive hunting depletes species and reduces their numbers. Tightening on prohibited places The Special Forces for Environmental Security renewed the warning against wild hunting in prohibited places, affirming that the violation carries a fine of 5,000 Saudi riyals, and calling for compliance with regulations and instructions on protecting the environment and wildlife. The tightening comes as the season continues until 31 January 2027, within a policy aimed at balancing regulated hunting with habitat conservation, especially during migration seasons. The Saudi experience holds particular importance in the Arab region, offering a model that combines the right to practice hunting with scientific regulation, monitoring, and species protection, at a time of growing need to develop the concept of responsible and sustainable hunting in the region.

articles.title: The planet’s skies are losing their balance: BirdLife sounds the alarm on global flyways
articles.body: A large flock of migratory birds crossing a wetland. BirdLife International — State of the World's Birds. Exclusive to Sayd Magazine | An editorial reading of the State of the World's Birds report Seasonal migration is no longer only a beautiful sight of flocks crossing the horizon as the seasons turn. It has become a precise vital sign of the planet’s pulse and the health of its ecosystems. In its latest edition, devoted entirely to intercontinental flyway networks, BirdLife International released its flagship report, revealing a dark and complex picture of what migratory birds are enduring. Their flocks face rising pressures that are redrawing the map of the world’s biodiversity. The bleed in numbers: 45% of species in continuous decline The report draws on a scientific database that assessed 1,843 migratory bird species worldwide. It finds that 45% of these species are recording a continuous numerical decline along their various routes, while only 14% are increasing, and 30% remain relatively stable. The data indicate that one in nine species (about 11%, or 200 species) is now globally threatened with extinction under the IUCN Red List. The degrees of risk break down as 32 species classified as Critically Endangered, 57 as Endangered, and 111 as Vulnerable, alongside dozens of other species close to the threat threshold — a sign that the crisis spans wide ecological groups. The most fragile groups: shorebirds and seabirds in the lead The report’s findings show that wetlands and marine environments are taking the hardest hit. Fifty-four percent of migratory shorebirds and waders are in sharp decline, as sabkhas are drained and coasts and tidal zones — vital refuelling stations before desert and sea crossings — are filled in. Forty-nine percent of seabird species face a similar drop because of bycatch in nets and fishing lines on the high seas, plus plastic pollution and the decline of fish stocks. Even birds once considered common in hunting and migration seasons, such as the European Turtle-dove and some ducks and coots, have suffered successive declines that have led to tighter international protections. Migratory European bee-eaters (Merops apiaster) on a thorny branch, one bird in flight — a colourful species of the Mediterranean flyways. Wikimedia Commons — CC BY-SA. Traps along the route: when wings meet infrastructure and human activity The report stresses that protecting a migratory bird in its breeding country alone does not guarantee its survival unless stopover sites and wintering grounds are equally safe. The main threats overlap along international routes: Habitat loss and degradation: more than 58% of 1,099 Key Biodiversity Areas (KBAs) are severely degraded by intensive agriculture, industry, and wetland drainage. Unregulated and illegal hunting: long coastal nets, electronic calling devices, and hunting outside permitted periods continue, especially at the Mediterranean and Middle East bottleneck, where estimates point to tens of millions of birds taken each year. Energy and wind corridors: wind farms and uninsulated high-voltage lines in narrow thermal corridors cause repeated collisions and electrocution of soaring birds such as eagles, storks, and falcons. Climate change and invasive species: the timing of food at arrival sites falls out of step, and rodents and other introduced animals prey on nests on remote islands. From diagnosis to rescue: a window of hope and the Nairobi Declaration The report does not stop at bleak numbers. It stresses that conservation science works when international efforts come together. The Global Flyways Summit adopted the Nairobi Flyways Declaration, under which governments and international development banks (including the World Bank) committed billions of dollars to protect wetland networks and restore safe routes. The clearest message BirdLife’s report sends to communities, people who love the wild, and hunters alike is that migratory birds cross political borders without passports. Keeping them requires moving from limited local protection to integrated, sustainable management along the entire flyway, so these flocks remain in our skies for generations to come.

articles.title: Smew
articles.body: Smew Mergellus albellus Identity and changing appearance Smew, Mergellus albellus, is a small northern diving duck, about 38–44 cm long. The adult male's white plumage is crossed by sharply contrasting black markings around the eye, on the head, back and breast. Its compact body and short, fine bill distinguish it from the larger, long-billed mergansers. At a distance the male may appear almost entirely white, so closer views are needed to appreciate the dark pattern and greyish flanks. Females have a chestnut-brown crown and nape, white cheeks and throat, and a grey body. Juveniles broadly resemble females, which is why the field term “redhead” does not necessarily identify a female. In the Naturalis description, juveniles have less dark in front of the eye and a duller wing patch. Males in eclipse also lose the striking winter contrast. Sex and age should therefore be recorded only as precisely as the view permits. A female Goldeneye is more robust and has a brown head without the Smew's broad white lower face. Female larger mergansers have longer bills and necks. In flight the Smew shows a conspicuous black-and-white wing pattern, with a smaller white patch in females. Size comparisons are most useful when the birds are at the same distance; a lone duck viewed across a wide reservoir can be misleading. Feeding and seasonal habitats On its breeding grounds, Smew combines two habitats that may seem unrelated: wooded country providing nest cavities, and freshwater providing food. Lakes, quiet rivers, pools and flooded woodland margins can all be used. In winter it often occupies lakes and reservoirs, and also sheltered coastal or brackish waters. Unlike a duck that merely requires an open nesting bank, it depends on the relationship between trees and water during reproduction. The bird feeds mainly by diving. Small fish dominate in winter and early spring, while aquatic insects and other invertebrates are more important in the breeding season. Prey may be brought to the surface before swallowing. The short bill is well suited to its small prey and should not be mistaken for the broad filtering bill of a dabbling duck. Feeding birds alternate submergence with short surface intervals, making patient, repeated observation more effective than a quick scan. Tree-hole breeding and young Smew nests in a tree cavity, often using an old woodpecker hole, including those made by Black Woodpeckers. It can also accept artificial nest boxes. The cavity is a protected chamber above ground, not an excuse to neglect the surrounding lake: the female and young need accessible, productive water after hatching. Old trees and safe feeding shallows thus form complementary parts of the breeding habitat. BTO gives a typical clutch of 7–9 eggs, with the female incubating for 26–28 days. The young are downy and precocial, meaning relatively well developed and mobile on hatching rather than helpless in a nest. Egg laying, incubation and brood rearing are distinct stages, and nesting dates vary across the broad northern range. A nest-box programme is appropriate only within a suitable breeding setting; installing a box at a southern wintering pond does not by itself create a breeding population. Eurasian range and winter movements The main breeding range lies in northern Europe and Asia. Birds leave northern breeding waters for more temperate wintering areas, with movements also occurring within winter when freezing closes feeding sites. Some winter movements are therefore responses to weather rather than a single fixed journey between two points. In western Europe, cold spells can bring birds farther west, while mild winters leave more open water closer to the breeding range. A study by Pavón-Jordán and colleagues, published in 2015, analysed counts from 16 European countries during 1990–2011. It documented a northeastward redistribution of wintering Smew associated with warmer conditions. This is a European finding, not a direct measurement of Arab populations, but it helps explain why fewer birds at one southern site need not indicate an equal decline throughout the range. Arab occurrence: national distinctions In Iraq, Salim and colleagues' checklist describes Smew as an uncommon winter visitor in the north and uncommon in the southern marshes. It also reports more than a thousand in the south in 1979, without a comparable subsequent occurrence in the evidence available to that publication. That exceptional historical count should not be presented as today's normal winter population. In Syria, Murdoch and Betton's 2008 checklist documents winter records from the Euphrates and Khabur reservoirs, including the first accepted observations in February 2004 and further records in 2006–2007. The authors suggested that it might winter regularly in the north, where observation coverage was poor. The records establish winter occurrence; the proposed regularity remains the authors' assessment, not a demonstrated annual census. Morocco's rare-bird committee classifies Smew as a Palearctic accidental visitor. Egypt's 2019 national checklist accepts it in category A, which establishes wild occurrence since 1950 but does not itself specify frequency or season. These different labels matter: a northern Iraqi winter visitor, a Syrian winter record and a Moroccan rarity should not be merged into a claim of widespread regular Arab wintering. Conservation and unobtrusive watching BTO reports global Least Concern status. Conservation nevertheless requires both cavity-bearing woodland in the breeding range and undisturbed open water in winter. The European redistribution study found that protected areas helped accommodate changing winter distribution, while identifying gaps in protection. Southern refuges can remain valuable during harsh winters even when used less often in mild ones. From a hide or distant bank, document the head pattern, bill shape, accompanying ducks and behaviour. Avoid approaching repeatedly between dives, which can interrupt feeding. For unusual national records, photographs and a dated locality are more valuable than an unsupported age or sex assignment. Protecting mature waterside trees and maintaining quiet feeding water addresses the two very different habitats on which this small duck depends. articles.title: Spotless Starling
articles.body: Spotless Starling Sturnus unicolor Identity and identification Spotless Starling Sturnus unicolor belongs to Sturnidae. Dark glossy plumage includes relatively long throat feathers. It generally lacks Common Starling’s heavy spotting, but breeding Common Starlings can also lose many spots. Feather structure, voice and location must therefore be combined. It is placed in the order Passeriformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour Farmland, pasture, orchards and towns provide habitat. It takes ground insects and larvae, adding fruit and seeds seasonally. Social birds form communal roosts and sing from exposed perches. Food proportions vary with season and resources. Breeding and parental care Nests occupy tree, rock and building cavities. Spain’s SEO/BirdLife account gives usually four or five eggs, incubation around 10–15 days and young flying at about 21–22 days, followed by further feeding. Two broods are possible. These breeding-range reference durations do not impose a Spanish calendar on the Maghreb. Range and Arab occurrence It occurs in the western Mediterranean, particularly Iberia, parts of the Maghreb and Mediterranean islands. North African occurrence makes it relevant to an Arab encyclopedia, but it is not another name for widespread Common Starling: the scientific identities are distinct. Seasonality and observation Mainly resident with local movements, it can be watched in November. Flocks may mix with wintering Common Starlings, requiring several individuals and angles to be documented. Lack of visible spots in a dark or distant photograph is insufficient. Ecological role and conservation It consumes agricultural invertebrates and disperses some fruit seeds, while sometimes visiting fruit crops. Cavities, varied farmland and reduced pesticides support populations. Local crop management should avoid destroying roosts or nests and harming mixed species. articles.title: Steppe Eagle
articles.body: Steppe Eagle Aquila nipalensis Identity and identification Steppe Eagle Aquila nipalensis belongs to Accipitridae. Large and brown, it has broad wings and a long gape reaching approximately the rear of the eye. Juveniles show pale wing bands. Distant separation from Tawny Eagle and other eagles is difficult; brown colour alone is insufficient. It is placed in the order Accipitriformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Endangered (EN). Habitat, food and behaviour Steppe and dry open country provide small mammals, birds and carrion. Winter birds may gather at concentrated food, including waste sites. Thermal soaring saves travel energy but makes routes sensitive to weather and time of day. Breeding and parental care Breeding nests stand on ground, rocks and sometimes structures or trees. The Peregrine Fund reports one to four eggs and incubation around 45 days; young begin flight around 55–65 days. Feather growth does not mean immediate independence. Prey and conditions influence breeding success. Range and Arab occurrence Asian steppe breeding areas connect through the Middle East to Arab, African and Asian wintering regions. Lebanon has scarce spring and autumn passage. Winter concentrations in Arabia do not establish Lebanese winter status. Seasonality and observation Lebanon’s checklist records passage in February–May and September–mid-November. November can coincide with the end of passage and arrival farther south. Assigning a photograph to an Arab locality requires independent geographic provenance; an identification image cannot document an individual’s route. Ecological role and conservation Electrocution, poisons, collisions and habitat loss are threats. Gathering around contaminated food can create collective risk. Insulating dangerous poles, reducing toxicants and preserving migration corridors are practical measures; accurately documenting mortality helps identify causes. articles.title: Syria tightens monitoring of illegal hunting during bird migration
articles.body: Syria: circular calls on governors to curb illegal hunting during bird migration and strengthen monitoring. On 12 November, Syria’s Ministry of Local Administration and Environment received raptors seized at Jousiyeh during an attempted smuggling operation towards Lebanon. Syrian Al-Ikhbariya reported that they would undergo veterinary checks, health assessments and care. Birds fit for release would return to their natural habitat only after rehabilitation and confirmation of their readiness. Syria’s Ministry of Local Administration and Environment issued a circular on Tuesday, 10 November 2026, asking governors, in their capacity as heads of local hunting councils, to tackle illegal hunting during the autumn bird migration and take legal action in coordination with the relevant authorities. According to the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA), the move aims to protect wildlife, particularly endangered species, and preserve biodiversity. In a related statement, Minister of Local Administration and Environment Mohammad Anjarani called on local administrative units to step up monitoring and coordination and take violations affecting birds and their migration routes seriously. In a post on his official Facebook page reported by the agency, the minister stressed that protecting birds requires community participation and commitment alongside the work of public institutions, and that safeguarding the environment protects future generations’ right to it. Monitoring during the migration season These instructions are particularly important as migratory birds pass through Syria and stop there to rest while travelling between Africa and Eurasia. Indiscriminate hunting threatens their journeys, as well as the roles they play in controlling insects and pests and dispersing seeds. A SANA report published on 27 October had documented an enforcement operation in the Nabk and Yabroud areas of rural Damascus, during which officers destroyed more than 500 metres of illegal nets and freed birds caught in them. The report highlighted the dangers of nets that do not distinguish between species and can cause injuries that prevent some birds from continuing their migration even after they are released. The new circular stresses enforcing hunting regulations and pursuing violations during the migration season. Sayd previously covered campaigns against illegal hunting in Syria in the October edition of Sayd Arab Radar. articles.title: Syrian Hunter Amani Al-Homsi: I Oppose Illegal Hunting… I Hope Syria Enacts a Hunting Law Fair to Nature and to the Hunter
articles.body: Amani Al-Homsi, hunter from Aleppo. Syria’s best-known woman hunter speaks to Sayd about passion without bloodlust, sexist comments, the need for a seasonal hunting law, and ethical practice that protects both hobby and nature. Syria’s most famous woman hunter embraces nature with a mother’s love and takes her quarry with a falcon’s skill — without hesitation. It is the balance of spirit and body, skill and knowledge: harmony between nature and the responsible human being. Amani, a daughter of Aleppo, whose children take pride in her in hunting clothes because they feel her strength and capability — and who has never disappointed them with a delicious meal prepared by her skilled hands. She said in the interview: The direct reasons that drew me into hunting were contact with hunters, my passion, and watching nature — not a love of killing any living creature. The most positive press comment that affected me was: “A queen from my country who managed to balance her household duties and her hobby, and was creative and distinctive.” Of course there are negative comments too, including: “A woman’s place is the kitchen.” I have only outperformed men at shooting fixed targets — which embarrasses some of them. In the Salamiyah area during the season for the zar‘i bird, men always lead. I keep my children away from hunting guns for their safety. The obsession with boasting and attracting attention is a social blight amplified by social media. Issuing a new, organised hunting law that respects seasons in Syria is a core concern for hunters there. Several meetings have taken place between international associations and official bodies to draft a new hunting law that considers both the environment and the hunter… and we wait. Hunting kit is essential for survival: water, food, a knife, and emergency gear. In dangerous areas such as deserts and forests, extra equipment is needed — a whistle, a flare, plus a mobile phone or radio. Most important: trips to such areas should be in a group, not alone. On one bird-hunting trip along a riverbank in Tartous Governorate I ended up fishing: I left my companions, swam, and caught fish — which made them laugh. Once I climbed a mountain in Tartous, slipped, and rolled five metres down over stones, leaves, and thorns. I had some bruises, but I will certainly repeat that trip later. Yes, a woman hunter’s presence among hunters helps curb illegal hunting. I have felt that in meetings and hunting lectures I joined: everyone tries to present a respectable image of themselves and of their knowledge of the difference between random shooting and responsible hunting that protects the hobby — and that is good. The only time I hunted outside Syria was in the Qaa area of Lebanon. I love hunting very much in my country. Syria is a hunting country par excellence, and I hope laws are issued soon that allow me to move and hunt in all regions as in other countries. My preferred game… thrush (samman) and duck. I call on hunters to practise ethical, humane hunting that does not harm nature and does not drive birds toward extinction. I hope that in our countries, as in many others, the hunter will also hunt with the lens — so that the relationship with nature is not only a relationship with the gun.

articles.title: Syrian Woodpecker
articles.body: Syrian Woodpecker Dendrocopos syriacus A woodpecker living among trees and people Syrian Woodpecker is a resident bird of open, tree-rich landscapes, from scattered woodland to orchards and old gardens. Its scientific name, Dendrocopos syriacus, places it in the woodpecker family Picidae, but does not mean it is confined to Syria: its range extends through parts of Europe, the Caucasus and western Asia. About 21–24 cm long, it combines black and white plumage with a pinkish-red undertail area. In an Arab landscape visited by many seasonal migrants, it offers a different story: a bird whose year-round life depends on the trees of its own region. In November it can be sought in its known habitats without waiting for a migration wave. Its autumn presence primarily reflects residency, although some individuals move locally. Calls may reveal it before it is seen on a trunk, while its undulating flight becomes conspicuous when it crosses between trees. Failure to find it on one visit does not establish that it has disappeared. Birds can move between separated patches of woodland and orchards. Identification, sex and age Prominent white shoulder patches stand out against the dark back, and pale markings cross the black wings. The face has an extensive white area. The black line running from the bill towards the breast does not close the white space behind the cheek as it does in Great Spotted Woodpecker. This open cheek pattern is particularly useful, supported by relatively little white on the outer tail feathers and a softer, pinker undertail area. Several features together are safer than judging size alone. An adult male has a red patch on the nape, absent in an adult female. Juveniles have red on the crown, so red on the head cannot by itself identify an adult male. Young birds can be especially confusing when compared with other woodpeckers. A side view of the head and a clear tail photograph help documentation, provided these are obtained without chasing the bird or tapping an occupied nest tree to force it into view. Arab distribution: local residency, not uniform occurrence In Syria the species is associated with woodland and orchards, including the coastal mountains, the Anti-Lebanon range and the surroundings of Damascus. Syrian references also record it around Aleppo and Ghouta. This is a patchwork of suitable environments, not continuous occupation of the whole country. In Palestine, the Mahmiyat platform describes it as common, and an older scientific study documents breeding in the Gaza Strip. That historical study alone cannot establish present bird numbers or the current condition of their habitats. Jordan BirdWatch's list, updated in May 2020, classes it as resident, and the organisation's work includes it among breeding birds of traditional, tree-rich farmland in northern Jordan. Iraq's annotated bird checklist records it in northern woodland. These environments differ from open deserts and wetlands. Inclusion on a national list therefore does not mean the species is available throughout that country, or that it arrives there as a winter visitor. Lebanon: documented breeding and care with historical evidence The Society for the Protection of Nature in Lebanon explains that a 1974 reference considered the species locally extirpated, before breeding was confirmed at Qammouha and Fneideq in 1995. Nesting was subsequently recorded between 1996 and 2005 at mountain sites and around Aammiq and Qaraoun, with dispersing birds observed in the Litani Valley. This history illustrates why a gap in records, or an old judgement of status, should not become a permanent description of a species. In its account published in 2021, the society describes a subsequent local decline and identifies tree cutting, disturbance, persecution and illegal hunting among the pressures. This should be read as a dated Lebanese assessment, not a new census of every Arab population. Likewise, global Least Concern status does not rule out the loss of nesting trees or reduced survival opportunities at individual sites. The global picture cannot replace repeated local monitoring. Old trees and a diet that follows available resources This woodpecker needs suitable trees within a network of habitats more than an unbroken expanse of dense forest. Traditional orchards, gardens with large trees, open woodland and village edges can provide food and potential cavities. European studies document substantial use of tree-rich farmland. Success there does not mean replacing all the old trees in an Arab orchard with small ones will preserve the same ecological function. Tree age and structure matter more than simply counting trunks. Its food includes insect larvae, beetles, ants and other invertebrates, found by pecking, picking prey and working at bark. It also eats seeds, fruit, walnuts and almonds, sometimes wedging an item in a crack to break it open. Plant food is a genuine part of its diet, not evidence that it has stopped eating insects. This variety provides options as resources change, including in autumn and winter, but cannot guarantee survival where trees and shelter disappear. From drumming to a cavity and eggs Repeated drumming communicates presence; not every sound made with the bill is feeding activity. During the breeding season the bird excavates a cavity in a suitable trunk or branch, often where the wood is easier to work. The entrance remains small compared with the chamber inside. Spring activities begin earlier in parts of the Levant than in some European regions. A Polish nesting calendar should therefore not be transferred unchanged to Lebanon or Palestine. General references describe clutches of about 3–7 eggs, with regional differences in average size. A study of 73 nests in southeastern Poland during 2003–2006 recorded clutches of two to seven eggs and incubation lasting 9–13 days. These are measurements from one population, illustrating the relatively rapid stage rather than promising one duration for every Arab nest. Both parents care for the young. Details of their division of labour and timing require repeated observation, not an inference from a single bird visiting a hole. Nestlings, independence and the rest of the year The chicks hatch inside the cavity and require regular feeding; they cannot fly when they emerge from the eggs. The Polish study recorded 24–30 days in the nest before departure. Dependence on the parents continues for a time after fledging, so a young bird sitting on a branch is not necessarily independent or abandoned. Young birds may later leave their birthplace, explaining some sightings away from usual breeding sites without requiring an assumption of long-distance migration. The presence of a hole does not guarantee successful breeding. Other species may compete for cavities, and the same study documented a contribution from starlings to nest losses at its site. Retaining trees of different ages and alternative cavities therefore benefits the bird community. Holes should not be blocked simply because one appears unused. Outside the nesting season, access to food and shelter remains essential: these needs do not end when breeding is over. Protection and responsible observation Practical protection starts with retaining mature trees and safe areas of decaying wood where they pose no danger to people, and assessing pruning or felling before work begins. This does not mean leaving a hazardous tree untreated. It means combining public safety with habitat conservation through informed assessment. Careful pesticide management also helps: a bird that feeds on invertebrates needs accessible prey, not merely trees that look green but support little life. Watch from a steady distance, keep the flight path to the cavity clear, and retreat if adults stop approaching or repeatedly give alarm calls. Do not place food near a nest to attract a bird for a photograph, or remove healthy young from their surroundings. Records are more useful when they include habitat, date, behaviour and numbers, while protecting precise nest locations. Global Least Concern status is neither permission to hunt nor a substitute for local law. Photo: Лариса Артемьева / iNaturalist (CC0 1.0)

articles.title: Hunting law in the UAE: federal protection and local falconry rules
articles.body: Federal wildlife protection and Abu Dhabi’s local falconry rules, with the limits of local permits explained. Al Jahili Fort in Al Ain, United Arab Emirates Terrestrial hunting in the United Arab Emirates sits within federal wildlife legislation and emirate-level rules. Understanding whether an activity is permitted requires checking the species, location, method, season and licence together. Abu Dhabi’s falconry arrangements should never be presented as permission to hunt throughout the country. A foundational instrument is Federal Decree-Law No. 9 of 1983 regulating the hunting of birds and animals. It prohibits hunting specified animals, including gazelles, hares and spiny-tailed lizards. The protection attached to a species therefore matters before any hunting trip is considered. Federal legislation. Federal Law No. 24 of 1999 on environmental protection and development, amended by Law No. 11 of 2006, provides further safeguards. Article 12 prohibits hunting, killing or capturing listed birds and animals, protects nests and eggs, and requires authorisation for their possession, transport or sale as specified in the legislation. Environmental law and amendment. Within Abu Dhabi, Local Law No. 22 of 2005 regulates wild hunting. Its implementing regulations were issued under Resolution No. 69 of 2015 and amended by Resolution No. 5 of 2021. Environment Agency – Abu Dhabi licences specify the relevant seasons, areas and authorised species. Local regulatory amendment. Official open-area falconry rules restrict the quarry to captive-bred houbara bustards. Eligible licence applicants are UAE citizens aged at least 18, using registered falcons. Protected and restricted areas and prescribed separation distances must be respected. Damaging vegetation and transferring a licence to another person are prohibited. Agency falconry guidance. Weapons are separately regulated. Federal Decree-Law No. 17 of 2019 requires licences or permits for activities involving weapons. The legality of the proposed hunting activity and its method must therefore each be established. Official UAE government guidance. This is an explainer of established legislation, not a hunting-season announcement or legal advice. Before travelling, consult the relevant emirate authority, the latest seasonal decision and the actual licence conditions. A local permit has a defined scope; it does not create a nationwide hunting entitlement. articles.title: Eurasian Jackdaw
articles.body: Eurasian Jackdaw Coloeus monedula — Identification, habitats, breeding and seasonal occurrence in the Arab region Identity and recognition The Eurasian Jackdaw, also called the Western Jackdaw, Coloeus monedula, is a member of the crow family Corvidae. Older references may place it in Corvus as Corvus monedula. Compact and smaller than the larger crows, it has a relatively short bill, a dark cap and a silvery-grey nape and neck. Adults have conspicuously pale eyes contrasting with the dark head. Arabic sources sometimes call it “ghurab al-zarʿ”, a name that can also cause confusion with the Rook. The scientific name therefore remains important when matching regional names to species. Age and similar species Males and females look broadly alike: ordinary plumage photographs do not reliably establish sex. Young birds are browner, with a less strongly contrasting head; eye colour changes with age. Iris colour alone should not establish exact age or exclude a young Jackdaw. Identification should combine its compact build, short bill, grey neck and voice rather than a single colour. The Rook, Corvus frugilegus, is larger and longer-billed; it is a separate species despite similar vernacular names. Habitat, food and behaviour Jackdaws feed in fields, pastures and short grass, while tree holes, rocky cavities and old buildings provide nesting places. Noisy flocks and communal roosts are particularly noticeable outside the breeding season. Their varied diet includes invertebrates, seeds and fruit, sometimes eggs or nestlings. Much feeding takes place on the ground. A bird seen near buildings is not necessarily dependent on human refuse: suitable landscapes can combine open feeding areas with secure nesting cavities. Breeding and life cycle The nest is built inside a suitable cavity in a tree, rock face or building. British nest records indicate a typical single brood and four or five eggs. Female incubation lasts around twenty days, and young leave the nest at approximately 32 days. These approximate reference values come from British monitoring. Nesting dates vary with location and climate; the presence of an autumn flock is not evidence of local breeding. Arab-region distribution and seasonality Arab occurrence includes residents, winter visitors and rare records. Lebanon’s 2020 checklist describes a regular winter visitor from October to early March in the Beqaa, Anti-Lebanon and Marjaayoun, noting that reported residency lacks specific supporting evidence. Jordan’s list records residents and winter visitors; OSME’s 2024 regional list describes uncommon breeding in Iraq. Morocco’s 2010 checklist documented resident breeders and expansion through the northern Atlantic plains towards Rabat. The regional reference documents Kuwait’s first record in October 2023, contrasting with regular winter occurrence beginning in autumn in Lebanon. Ecology and conservation As a consumer of plant and animal food, the Jackdaw participates in several food webs. Its global category is Least Concern in the referenced Red List-based account, but this does not demonstrate that every local population is secure. Loss of cavities and changes in land use can reduce nesting or feeding opportunities. Protecting safe nesting sites and monitoring local populations are useful responses. articles.title: Western Rock Nuthatch
articles.body: Western Rock Nuthatch Sitta neumayer Identity, life and distribution Western Rock Nuthatch Sitta neumayer is a compact bird with grey upperparts, pale underparts and a dark eye stripe. It belongs to the nuthatch family, but rocky surfaces play a greater role in its life than woodland trunks. It moves nimbly over slopes, cliffs and crevices. Food includes insects, plant seeds and other invertebrates, with seasonal changes. It sometimes visits trees, so its perch alone is not an identification character. A mud-built nest occupies a fissure or sheltered rock overhang, with a narrow entrance. Do not touch the structure or linger in front of it; distant observation is enough to appreciate its construction. OSME documents resident occurrence in Lebanon, Syria and northeastern Iraq. It is distinct from Eastern Rock Nuthatch Sitta tephronota. Identification requires attention to both features and locality, especially where the species approach one another. www.oiseaux.net — Western Rock Nuthatch · www.osme.org — Western Rock Nuthatch · wildlebanon.org — Western Rock Nuthatch Photo: James Eaton

articles.title: When Autumn Becomes a Season for Hunting Images
articles.body: Source: Mecshap From the rifle to the lens: how journalism can help protect migratory birds and change the culture of displaying kills. Golden leaves are not the only things that fall in Lebanon’s autumn. Birds that should be crossing its skies on their way to Africa sometimes fall too, discovering that a stopover has become an ambush. Storks and birds of prey arrive along their migration routes, only to be met by some people with a rifle and a phone: the first to bring down the bird, the second to immortalise a false feat of heroism. As though hitting a creature exhausted by its journey required an applauding audience. This is precisely where the philosophy promoted by Sayd Magazine comes into focus: ‘hunting the image instead of the bird’. It does not extinguish the passion for pursuit and challenge, but gives it a nobler spirit, replacing the rifle with a lens and camouflage for killing with camouflage for documenting. It allows the bird to live and continue its journey. Lebanon is an important passage for migratory birds travelling between Europe, Asia and Africa. Flocks gather along corridors that make them more vulnerable to being targeted. Protecting them goes beyond compassion for a broken wing: depending on their species, birds help control pests, disperse seeds and maintain ecological balance. Their repeated loss is therefore a loss for nature and agriculture alike. Everyone has a part to play in the cycle of protection that allows birds to pass safely, and the media must provide a broad platform for that effort. Through reporting, broadcasting and public awareness, they can make this loss understandable, moving birds beyond the category of beautiful scenery and showing how their lives serve a function in nature. Coverage that stops at a photograph of a slaughtered flock before moving to the next story may create a passing shock, while leaving the culture that produced the scene comfortably in place. The image itself carries a striking paradox. A study published by André Raine and colleagues in Oryx in February 2025 analysed approximately 1,844 photographs posted on Facebook and Instagram between 2011 and 2023. Researchers identified 212 species of hunted birds, 94% of which were legally protected in Lebanon. Photographs intended for boasting thus became evidence documenting violations: the irresponsible hunter displays an achievement, while the researcher reads a record of an offence. One article will not stop every rifle. But the media can withdraw the applause surrounding it. From awareness to follow-up Such coverage has value in building knowledge, but statements need more follow-up on the ground: where are the nets set? How are birds sold? And what happens after a violation is detected? Media follow-up in Lebanon could improve through regular coverage that begins before autumn migration, explains protected species and hunting rules in clear language, and includes experts and law-abiding hunters. Television and digital platforms can tell stories of rescue and birdwatching, while avoiding precise disclosure of sensitive species’ locations or presenting killing footage as entertainment. The media can thus play a vital and influential role in protecting migratory birds in Lebanon. One initiative would be to challenge ‘hunting for engagement’ through parallel campaigns that present wildlife documentarians and environmental advocates as the real heroes, highlighting images of birds flying free as a constructive alternative to photographs of killing and abuse. It is important to move beyond emotional awareness towards economic and agricultural understanding, producing investigative reports and accessible media material about migratory birds’ ecological roles. Explaining how birds of prey and storks help control rodents and agricultural pests, for example, can show citizens and farmers that killing these birds causes direct material and economic losses for the country. Developing environmental investigative journalism and field monitoring could be a particularly important initiative. Investigations could use open-source tools to trace videos and leaked material documenting the mass killing of migratory birds, and hold social media platforms and the relevant authorities to account for shortcomings in enforcing the law and restricting this content. Media partnerships with schools and field organisations may also be among the most effective long-term initiatives. Interactive content for young people—short stories, interactive documentaries and programmes on TikTok and Instagram—could be created with environmental experts and civil society organisations, spreading a culture of birdwatching tourism as a promising source of economic and tourism activity for Lebanon. One article will not stop every rifle. But the media can withdraw the applause surrounding it and turn a violation into an issue that persists after the video disappears. Autumn can then become a season for watching the travellers in our skies, and birds can stop paying the price for a human desire to be seen.

articles.title: When You Humiliate Your Quarry… You Humiliate Yourself!
articles.body: Respect for quarry is the true test of a hunter’s ethics In Lebanon, where hunting is part of our heritage, culture and relationship with nature, we sometimes witness distressing behaviour by hunters who treat their quarry with hostility and contempt after killing it. They violently fling a bird from their hands, slam it against the ground or kick it, as though facing an enemy they wish to humiliate and proclaim victory over, even after its life has ended. Such scenes suggest that the shot that killed the bird was not enough to satisfy their sense of superiority, so they vented the rest of their aggression on a helpless body. Moments earlier, this bird was a living creature, flying and searching for food. It may have travelled thousands of kilometres on an arduous migration, facing storms and dangers before its life ended with a shot. Does this creature lose its value and its claim to respect simply because it falls dead? In long-established hunting cultures, respect for quarry holds a special place. Some peoples have even developed rituals and traditions to honour the animals they hunt. In Germany, hunters maintain a tradition known as Letzter Bissen, or the “last bite”, in which a small green branch is placed in the mouth of certain wild animals taken in the hunt, as an expression of respect for the life that has been taken. In the traditions of collective hunts, the quarry is carefully laid out and special hunting-horn calls are played in its honour. Stepping over the bodies is considered disgraceful behaviour that goes against inherited customs. In Japan, the Matagi hunters were known for their traditional bear-hunting rituals. After killing an animal, they would offer special prayers and perform ceremonies expressing their spiritual beliefs and respect for nature. In New Zealand, the code of ethics for game-bird hunting stresses the need to retrieve and care for quarry, avoid waste and kill no more than is needed. In Britain, hunting organisations emphasise proper handling of shot birds and avoiding piling them up in ways that cause spoilage, on the principle of respecting and preserving the quarry. Customs and rituals differ between peoples, but they meet around one ethical principle: the life you have taken deserves respect even after it has ended. The Lebanese hunter does not need to imitate these rituals or adopt other people’s beliefs. Respect for quarry does not require ceremonial observances. It is enough to carry it carefully, preserve it and refuse to turn its death into a scene of mockery or showing off. Hunting culture reveals itself in a hunter’s behaviour when alone in nature, in the way the hunter treats the quarry when cameras are absent, and in the respect taught to children and to new hunters who accompany them. You may carry the most expensive gun in the world, wear the finest hunting clothes and own the latest optics and equipment. Your hand may be steady and your eye so accurate that you hardly ever miss a target. But all these capabilities lose their value when respect is absent from your conduct. The true test of a hunter’s ethics begins after the quarry falls. If you are incapable of respecting your quarry, do not consider yourself a hunter. Photo: Social media.

articles.title: White-eared Bulbul
articles.body: White-eared Bulbul Pycnonotus leucotis Identity and identification White-eared Bulbul Pycnonotus leucotis belongs to Pycnonotidae. A black head bears large white cheek patches above a grey-brown body and yellow undertail. Those patches differ from White-spectacled Bulbul’s narrow eye-ring. Yellow undertail colour alone does not identify either species. It is placed in the order Passeriformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour Orchards, gardens, oases and wooded farmland provide habitat. Fruit, seeds and insects are eaten in pairs or small groups. Association with people does not mean dependence on handouts: fruiting trees and invertebrates remain natural resources. Breeding and parental care A cup nest occupies a shrub or tree, including palms. Iraqi references document small clutches of up to three eggs and parental provisioning. Dates vary among regions. Captive-breeding observations should not be presented as measurements from wild populations. Range and Arab occurrence Its range extends from southwestern Asia into parts of the Gulf. It is familiar in Iraq and Bahrain; Saudi sources describe a common breeding resident. Native and introduced populations may coexist regionally, so origin should be stated when established rather than assuming every record reflects natural spread. Seasonality and observation Resident sites support year-round sightings, including November. Document cheek-patch extent, head and tail with location. An isolated bird beyond its expected range does not automatically prove natural expansion or breeding; escape from captivity may need exclusion. Ecological role and conservation Fruit and insect consumption contribute to food webs and some seed dispersal. Illegal capture and trade, pesticides and loss of varied gardens are pressures. Native planting and avoiding ornamental capture help, while indiscriminate releases of captive birds should be avoided. References B. E. articles.title: White Stork — Ciconia ciconia
articles.body: White storkSayd Magazine archive Range: A large bird with white wings tipped black, and red bill and legs. It breeds across Europe, North Africa, and western Asia, and winters mainly in sub-Saharan Africa. Its eastern flyway runs through Turkey, the Levant, and the Nile Valley; Lebanon is part of the Levantine bottleneck for soaring migrants between Europe and Africa. It is told from the black stork Ciconia nigra by its mostly white plumage and red bill. Life cycle and habitat: Socially monogamous in the season; the male arrives early and chooses the bulky stick nest, often reused for years on trees, rooftops, or platforms. The female typically lays about four eggs; incubation lasts roughly 33–34 days with both parents sharing; hatching is asynchronous. The parents feed the young; fledging follows after about 58–64 days. It forages in damp meadows, shallow farmland, and pools: insects, worms, amphibians, small reptiles, rodents, and sometimes fish or nestling birds. Lifestyle: Gregarious on migration and in winter gatherings; more territorial at the nest. The famous bill-clattering, amplified by the throat pouch, is its social signal. It climbs on warm air then glides long distances, saving energy against continuous flapping; it avoids long Mediterranean sea crossings because thermals form poorly over water. Hence the preference for land bridges and bottlenecks—among them Lebanese skies at peak seasons. White storkSayd Magazine archive Hunting status: Across Arab countries, hunting white stork is generally prohibited unless a specific state issues an official seasonal decree that expressly lists it. In Lebanon, Wild Hunting Law No. 580/2004 limits hunting to quarry species set by the minister; everything else is protected year-round; white stork is not among the permitted quarry in the absence of a current open-season decision. Conservation status: Globally Least Concern with the International Union for Conservation of Nature, with an increasing trend in parts of Europe thanks to protection programs. It remains exposed to wetland loss, power lines, and illegal shooting on some flyways. Traits: A lesson in flight economy. Its massive nest can become a living structure that sometimes hosts smaller birds. Bill-clattering is a clear social message without complex song. Over Lebanon it passes as an emblem of the eastern–African migration corridor.

articles.title: White-throated Kingfisher
articles.body: White-throated Kingfisher Halcyon smyrnensis Identity and identification White-throated Kingfisher Halcyon smyrnensis belongs to Alcedinidae. Chestnut head and body contrast with a white throat and breast, blue back and wings and a large red bill. It differs conspicuously from smaller Common Kingfisher and black-and-white Pied Kingfisher. The sexes look alike in the field. It is placed in the order Coraciiformes. The IUCN category carried in AviList 2026 is Least Concern (LC). Habitat, food and behaviour It is not confined to water margins, using farmland, orchards and open ground near channels. From a branch or wire it watches and dives onto prey. Large insects, lizards, amphibians and other small animals supplement available fish; it is not exclusively a fish eater. Breeding and parental care A tunnel excavated into an earthen bank ends in an egg chamber. References report clutches of three to seven eggs. Both parents incubate and provision young inside the chamber. Chicks develop in the nest before emerging; opening a tunnel for photography destroys necessary protection. Range and Arab occurrence Its range extends from the eastern Mediterranean through parts of the Middle East to southern Asia. Lebanon’s 2020 checklist records it in most months without then confirming breeding. Documented occurrence should therefore be distinguished from a claim of proven Lebanese breeding residence. Seasonality and observation It can be observed throughout the year in resident areas. Loud calls and exposed lookout perches aid detection. A November sighting at an eastern site alone does not reveal whether an individual is resident or moving; observations across seasons are more informative. Ecological role and conservation Its varied prey connects it to agricultural food webs. Bank levelling removes nesting opportunities, while pesticides and polluted water are pressures. Stable earthen banks, safe perches and varied vegetation support the bird without disturbing nests. articles.title: Wings reclaim the sky… Tamara El Zein visits Zgharta’s bird rescue centre
articles.body: White storks at the Lebanese Association for Migratory Birds’ site, where injured birds receive care and rehabilitation before returning to the wild when their condition allows. Environment Minister Dr Tamara El Zein visited the Lebanese Association for Migratory Birds’ centre in Jerjour, in the district of Zgharta, to learn about efforts to rescue, care for and rehabilitate injured birds for their return to the wild. The visit included the release of treated and rehabilitated birds in Horsh Ehden Nature Reserve to mark World Migratory Bird Day. The programme also included an environmental tour of the reserve to explore its biodiversity and natural riches, before concluding with the opening of an insect exhibition. Environment Minister Tamara El Zein taking part in the release of birds following treatment and rehabilitation, during her visit to the association and Horsh Ehden Nature Reserve. From injury to another chance to fly The visit highlights work that extends beyond the moment of release: receiving an injured bird, providing appropriate care and monitoring its recovery until it can return to the wild. The association’s centre, headed by Dr Michel Sawan, receives wild birds of different species, including raptors and storks. Care involves isolating cases when necessary, treating wounds and fractures, and rehabilitation. Injuries that cause permanent disability may prevent a bird’s release, in which case its care continues within the association’s facilities. Images from the site show a group of white storks in a fenced care area — a scene that captures the centre’s role as a place to regain strength before a possible return to the sky. Storks and raptors return to the wild During 2025 and 2026, the association’s activities documented other milestones in returning birds to nature. On 5 April 2025, it organised a release with the Polish Embassy in Beirut, including storks that had undergone lengthy rehabilitation after being rescued from illegal hunting. In June 2026, the release of a honey buzzard was announced in cooperation with the municipality of Metrit in Koura, after the bird received care at the association’s shelter and recovered from its injury. The event conveyed a message about protecting raptors and their role in agricultural ecosystems, while connecting bird rescue with local community participation. Feliks… a rescue journey across borders Among the most striking stories to emerge in 2026 was that of Feliks, an eastern imperial eagle that set off from Serbia and reached Syria, where it fell into the hands of illegal hunters. The Lebanese Association for Migratory Birds helped rescue him. He spent more than six months at a shelter in northern Lebanon before returning to Serbia. There, a specialist team continued his care and flight training until he was released near Subotica on 6 August 2026. Tracking showed that within days he had reached the Slovak–Polish border. This story illustrates how protecting a migratory bird may require cooperation across countries: its route connects regions and nations that share responsibility for keeping it safe. Protection continues after release Alongside rescue, the association raises awareness of the value of wildlife. In July 2025, it worked with the North Lebanon Agriculture Department on a seminar in Danniyeh about the role of birds and wild animals in protecting crops and forests. The environment minister’s visit brings these elements together: care within the centre, a return to nature and attention to reserves and biodiversity. Yet the rescue journey does not end when a bird spreads its wings. Its safety still depends on protecting habitats and migration routes, respecting hunting laws and preventing attacks on protected species. articles.title: Yellowhammer
articles.body: Yellowhammer Emberiza citrinella Identity, life and distribution Yellowhammer Emberiza citrinella is a bunting with a short seed-handling bill. Males show a conspicuously yellow head; females are more streaked and subdued. Head pattern and rump should be checked together when separating it from Cirl Bunting. Farmland, woodland edges and hedges provide habitat. Seeds are important food, alongside invertebrates. Trees alone do not make suitable habitat: birds also need a combination of vegetation cover and open feeding ground. The nest is on or close to the ground in dense vegetation. BTO reports a typical clutch of three or four eggs. Grassy margins and short, thick hedges provide shelter for nesting birds. RSPB links British declines to insufficient food and nesting habitat. Seed-rich winter stubbles and protected field margins illustrate practical habitat management. The British trend does not establish population trends in Arab countries. In the Maghreb it is rare or accidental; a specialist Algerian report from 2024 discusses the scarcity of regional records. www.bto.org — Yellowhammer · www.rspb.org.uk — Yellowhammer · www.rspb.org.uk — Yellowhammer · magornitho.org — Yellowhammer Photo: steve b
